Building upon previous research into the facet rotation method for linear programming, we made two key contributions. Firstly, we established a theoretical guarantee for the proposed algorithm by proving that the facet rotation method generates a convergent sequence of optimal solutions with a bounded iteration limit. Secondly, we substantiated the efficacy of the facet rotation method by demonstrating through experimentation that it yields solution times that substantially surpass the absolute limit imposed by computational precision when applied to randomly generated problems within a defined realm of dimensions and facet counts, with performance ratios consistently fluctuating between 25 to 135 times greater depending on varying parameters, with an average ratio of about 31.

We introduce a dual notion, NK_1, of Bak's unitary collection (U_t)^{oo} to study properties of graded rings with the NK_1 property. Our main findings include defining graded NK_1 rings, exploring their characteristics on a graded R, and proving that Bak and graded NK_1 properties are equivalent through graded extension. Additionally, we investigate the relationship between the NK_1 property in upper and lower graded series. Furthermore, we define Bak's W_t and demonstrate that in some cases, NK_1 is equivalent to the W_t property. Our research also explores duality in Bak's unitary collection and reveals that NK_1 is reflectable across dual rings. Lastly, we define Bak's Q_t and establish a relationship chain from Bak's (U_t)^{oo} to NK_1, Q_t, and Q_1.

This paper investigates the influence of off-shell contributions within the top quark production framework, specifically in ttj events, on the top quark mass (m_t) determination. A detailed theoretical examination is conducted within a fixed-order framework with next-to-leading order accuracy, accompanied by an investigation into whether an partial next-to-leading order correction with an on-shell top quark assumption can adequately account for the off-shell effects. Experimental validation is carried out via a parton-level generator with an next-to-leading order accuracy match and an algebraic phase-space phase matching. The findings suggest that a m_t correction of approximately 10 GeV is required to account for the absence of these off-shell contributions. However, the research further discovers that such a correction is only fully utilised in the event samples with the lowest m_t kinematical ranges. The findings emphasize the m_t correction dependence on the m_t sample considered. The study's proposals are intended for use within the CMS experiment, specifically within the field of weak-boson production off a light top quark within a hadronic final stage.

The effectiveness of Vision Transformer (ViT) models is being recognized in various computer vision tasks, thanks to their ability to accept fixed-size input images in a pre-trained state. When it comes to zero-shot face anti-spoofing, using a ViT model means not needing to fine-tune on specific attack types. A critical element in achieving this high level of efficiency is the tokenization process, which greatly affects the comparison of ViT models. This study addresses the lack of consistency in existing tokenization methods, proposing a new feature splitting approach to better capture spatial and temporal aspects of facial data. By exploring the impact of tokenization, new features' length, and model architecture on performance, this research builds a comprehensive benchmark for further research and compares the efficacy of ViT models in zero-shot face anti-spoofing, an area where previous studies have been lacking in depth.

Deep Reinforcement Learning has shown significant potential in tackling complex AI challenges. Considering the diverse capabilities of DRL algorithms, which incorporate both supervised and imitation learning elements, our research aims to explore its feasibility in developing an autonomous self-driving system. We'll be working with the collection of datasets from sensor data, traffic rules, and GPS navigation as well as the integration of DRL algorithms to control the vehicle. Since a vehicle operating in real-world conditions must adhere to traffic laws, our work will specifically involve Policy-Based DRL techniques to optimize lane and positioning controls in conjunction with GPS data and a proposed tremapolicy to monitor and maintain consistent velocity. We'll examine various policy-based approaches, such as Constant Policy, Gaussian Policy, and Intention Policy, in conjunction with an Attention Transformer, and evaluate them against proven DRL algorithms like Soft Actor Critic and Impressive Loss. Given the various parameters involved in optimizing performance, our research aims to demonstrate the efficacy of velocity as a crucial factor in optimizing rewards and reducing training objectives. We'll conduct an in-depth analysis of a hybrid tremapolicy incorporating the above-mentioned factors and prove its capability to train effectively with a relatively small number of real-time data samples. Notably, our research will be supported by high-level design diagrams, detailed coding snippets, and experimental results, and we hope to contribute to the development of a self-driving system utilizing DRL technology.

Evolutionary algorithms have seen significant advancements in recent years through parallel computing, particularly in tackling complex multi-objective optimization problems.  However, a major limitation in their effectiveness lies in the variable time required for evaluating candidate solutions. This inefficiency is exacerbated when utilizing a centralized, asynchronous approach, leading to potentially inferior outcomes. To address this constraint, this research introduces a novel parent selection method based on frequency to mitigate the effects of evaluation time bias in asynchronous, multi-objective evolutionary algorithms. By leveraging an unbiased, dynamic archive to record unique solution evaluations, this approach counts the frequency of each solution's parentage, guiding the selection of parents. As an archive with an unlimited capacity can potentially solve any optimization problem, its impact on the overall algorithm remains minimal. Moreover, all key components of the algorithm, including its parent selection method, can be viewed as unbiased, comprehensive archive management. To evaluate its effectiveness, two challenging optimization problems are employed and a comprehensive comparison is conducted against a state-of-the-art, asynchronous, multi-objective evolutionary algorithm. Results demonstrate that the parent selection method proposed here can significantly enhance quality of the resulting Pareto-frontiers and, in certain scenarios, find better solutions than the standard approach.

The binary source identification problem has been a major obstacle in interpreting long timescale microlensing planets. Researchers have made significant progress in understanding this challenge, particularly in employing the gravitational influence on nearby stars as an indicator of planetary gravity. Our study specifically examines the binary source identification hurdle in relation to a previously discovered planet, OGLE-2017-BLG-1434L, which was initially reported with an uncertain mass-to-radius ratio. To further analyze this planet, we utilized the SWEPAM instrument on the Keck telescope to measure the gravitational influence on nearby stars along the lensing direction, thereby confirming the existence of the planet at a mass of 0.5 M_Earth and a low mass-to-radius ratio of 0.2. This finding not only resolves the binary source identification problem but also demonstrates the potential of the SWEPAM technique in gravitational lensing, which may become a major technique for detecting and characterizing planets in the future large scale microlensing experiments.

We examine the high-frequency behavior of time-asymmetric Lindblad evolution, 
a form of non-unitary dynamics distinct from the standard high-frequency expansion 
used in classical perturbation theory and in uncoupled quantum dynamics. 
Our analysis shows that in high-frequency scenarios, the expansion of the 
Lindblad generator up to a specific order must be consistent across rotating-wave 
and counter-rotating interactions. Additionally, we had to adapt our method to account 
for the non-standard structure of the Lindblad equation. Using our derived expansion, 
we can analyze the effects of high-frequency detunings, raw high-frequency rotating-wave 
terms, and high-frequency back-action from fast oscillations. Our study specifically 
investigates the dynamics of two-level systems and superposition-like states, revealing 
key differences in their behaviors. This work lays a groundwork for expanded analysis of 
multi-level systems.

Our recent studies of the effects of Rh content in the alloy CePd$_{1-x}$Rh$_x$ using polarized neutrons revealed the appearance of ferromagnetic and spin-freezing behavior within the alloy's crystalline structure. At very low concentrations of Rh, the alloy exhibited traditional paramagnetic properties; however, at a critical concentration of approximately $x$, a type of commensurate collinear ferromagnetism developed, which shifted to become incommensurate upon further increasing the Rh content. Notably, at an intermediate concentration of Rh between 0.25 and 0.65, the alloy displayed both long-range magnetic order and local spin-freezing behaviors, which could be perceived through the way they interfere with one another. Using specialized analysis software, we were able to accurately model the observed neutron depolarization patterns in all the alloy samples, which provided us with valuable information about the actual alignment of the magnetic dipole moments. Our findings suggest that the alignment of the magnetic dipole moments within the alloy CePd$_{1-x}$Rh$_x$ is largely influenced by the alloy's structural properties.

Data from the Green Bank Telescope's Galactic Plane Survey have been analyzed to examine a high-mass star-forming region labeled G176.51+00.20. Research has revealed two factors that contribute to the region's 21 cm emission, specifically, a compact high-speed jet originating from a protostar and external ionizing events. The study employed the Gaussian Process emulator to accurately model the region's spectral characteristics. Observations showed a high-speed jet with minimal width that travels at an average speed of 140 km/s over approximately 0.5 parsecs. This is consistent with jets from young, high-mass objects. The study also found that external ionizing events are responsible for a broader, 70 km/s outflow that surrounds the region's stellar disk. Furthermore, research suggested that these ionizing events may play a crucial role in the region's star formation process, specifically through the compression of surrounding gas.

We demonstrate the topological equivalence of all intermediate beta-transformations with a specific type of greedy beta-transformation that has gaps, by leveraging a new form of interwinding that combines combinatorial elements with fractional ones, and by establishing it as the product of a family of simple to construct one-dimensional pieces, thereby providing a new classification for these intermediate transformations. Additionally, this research introduces a new method for characterizing topologically distinct systems that have similar behavior at their boundaries. This finding has significant implications as it implies the systems characterized by Adler, McIntosh, and Shields, that have similar orbit behavior, are actually topologically equivalent systems.

Determining the CP-violating phase phi_s resulting from mixing-induced phenomena in Bs decays is a crucial method for discovering potential new physics phenomena. Utilizing approximately 7,421 +/- 105 signal events from predominantly hadronic Bs J/\psi pi+ rho- decays, which were isolated in a 1 fb-1 dataset of pp collision data collected at a 7 TeV energy level, researchers found phi_s to be approximately -0.019 +/- 0.017 +/- 0.004, in agreement with the Standard Model's predicted value.

Deep neural networks have exhibited remarkable performance across a wide array of image classification tasks. However, due to their inherent bias towards specific data sets, they often struggle when applied to unrelated domains. This knowledge gap highlights the significance of domain adaptation methods, which aim to improve neural network performance by adapting it to a new, untained dataset. Inspired by the commonalities between humans learning concepts from everyday experiences, we have developed and investigated domain adaptation methods that mimic natural learning processes. Specifically, we have assessed the efficacy of transfer learning, pseudo-label techniques, and semi-supervised learning in adapting deep neural networks. Furthermore, we have demonstrated the practical value of these methods in enhancing image recognition across various gender and embryo classification tasks.

Consider curves in two-dimensional finite fields of odd prime order, and define a curve of maximal smoothness as one with no singular points and whose decomposition along places does not exceed its geometric genus. A specific result asserts that such maximally smooth curves have a counting process with an asymptotic lower limit that can be expressed as the product of the field's characteristic and a specific constant, which depends on the curve's genus and remains constant as the field's order increases. This result reflects a general extension of previous findings by Lefschetz in algebraic topology applied to curves in these fields. These findings also imply that curves of a given maximal smoothness are predominantly represented in the curve's geometric counterpart. Additionally, we show that the counting process for such curves can be expressed as the product of the field's characteristic and a specific constant, which reflects the intersection of two divisor classes, one associated with the curve itself and another with its dual.
A proof without words shows that there are $\binom{3^n}{4}$ equilateral triangles in the tetrahedral grid by recursively counting them in a unique triangular formation.

Graph Neural Networks, a highly effective model for tabular and graph-structured data, struggle with performance when applied to datasets with mixed data types and large character limits, primarily due to the implementation in Python. Our research focuses on optimizing GNN for multi-instance datasets with up to 256 fields by using a compiled, numerical approach. This involves representing fields as fixed-size byte arrays and processing them using a hash function that is based on the specific GNN operator. Our experiment reveals that processing fields as bytes prevents evaluation overhead, resulting in a significant runtime improvement. Specifically, our findings indicate that processing fields at the node or graph level leads to a performance gain of 1.5 to 2 times, while an additional improvement of 40% can be achieved if we apply early hashing using the GNN operator's hash function. Our research also includes an open-source tool that allows users to compile and run GNN programs on a target dataset, optimizing performance for specific hardware configurations such as GPU, CPU, or memory constraints.

The peculiar system, RXCJ0232.2-4420, at $z$ = 0.28, contains a unique radio halo surrounding its central cluster core, which is surrounded by a jet-like radio structure. To gain insights into its dynamics and the large-scale environment, we examined the morphological characteristics of its gas through optical data and analyzed its two-dimensional spatial properties on a substructure level using, specifically, $m_{500}$ as a reference. By applying scaling relations and considering possible influences from outside, we aimed to characterize the thermal and non-thermal components of the cluster's gas. Furthermore, we investigated the substructure levels within a 1 Mpc radius around the core and evaluated the reliability of cosmological constraints derived from this system. Our results indicate that only two out of nine examined parameters show significant correlations with radius, consistent with hydrostatic equilibrium assumptions. Nonetheless, the large dispersion in our data hinders our ability to derive reliable values for $Y_{X}$, particularly when compared to Dwarakanath et al. (2010). Furthermore, the large-scale environment was found to possibly affect the system's properties. While our findings support the reliability of the peculiar system as a probe for cosmological investigations, the uncertainties within this particular parameter prevent it from being used to derive the cosmological $\sigma_8$. Furthermore, the substructure levels within a 1 Mpc radius around the core suggest that the system may not be in a completely relaxed state.

The performance of neural networks can be significantly enhanced by incorporating orthogonalization through the Legendre memory block (LMB) technique, making it a valuable tool for improving long-term recurrent models. Despite the potential of LMB, training models with this method is a time-consuming and computationally demanding process due to its high matrix multiplication cost and linearity. We have developed an LMB parallelization technique for GPU implementation, which involves partitioning the memory block and leveraging linearization to optimize training efficiency. The effectiveness of our method has been validated on multiple long-term neural sequences, resulting in a notable speedup in training time for LSTM and GRU models on a variety of tasks.

For over a century, discoveries of particles with no interparticle interaction have been made, including neutrinos, which were long thought to be unchanged by interactions, until recently revised. The search for even more elusive particles with extremely weak interactions is ongoing using advanced experimental techniques across various fronts, including cosmic rays, deep underground locations, and powerful particle accelerators, all aimed at uncovering new physics beyond the established Standard Model of particle interactions. This review explores the motivations, experiments, and evidence from astrophysical, terrestrial, and laboratory studies for discovering particles with minimal interparticle interactions that might also explain new phenomena observed in nature, such as cosmic rays and gravitational anomalies, and could potentially unveil new physics beyond the established Standard Model of particle interactions, involving additional Higgs fields, scale or contact interactions, and so on.

Langton's naming game serves as a straightforward model for understanding the emergence of language. In the original version of this model, agents with identical goals interact in groups, aiming to achieve consensus on a single concept using three values. In a dynamic system where agent interactions are short-term and flexible, agent pairs develop shared understanding by matching their values. Although value matching is a straightforward goal-driven approach, it might lead some agents to have different understanding than others within the same group, resulting in diversity of knowledge despite being in the same group. However, when agents are mobile and can move freely, groupings of agents consensually develop their own unique languages due to their goal-driven goal of matching values. In contrast, a system where agent interactions are restricted, results in a different dynamic where diverse knowledge coexists. Interestingly, mobile agents can also achieve consensus on unique languages when they have similar goals. These shared goals enable consensually consistent languages to emerge, unlike the game-driven, equitable values that lead to consistent languages without requiring equity.

Research into neural networks' ability to learn from noisy data has led to a general understanding that their performance improves as their size increases, but a floor is reached where their performance no longer significantly improves with increased size. This phenomenon, attributed to spectral bias, occurs when a network's predicted outputs fail to capture relevant high-frequency information. In this study, we investigate how using momentum when training physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) to solve partial differential equations reduces the impact of spectral bias. We find that incorporating momentum into the loss function is an efficient way to overcome spectral bias, and we demonstrate this by comparing the network's ability to approximate a solution on a grid of increasingly finer grids. As the grid resolves more complex solutions, the method using momentum yields more accurate results that closely match the actual solution.

We examine a two-wave system that interacts with each other and is affected by viscoelastic damping in specific regions, then extend this analysis to a more comprehensive model that includes coupled wave equations in the entire space. By employing dynamic stability principles, we determine that small viscoelastic damping is sufficient for the system to maintain stability and exponential energy dissipation. This investigation is motivated by an issue in acoustic scattering, where a wave interacts with a viscoelastic absorber that has gaps in it.

Reinforcement learning without explicit guidance has limitations in certain tasks involving scarce data. As a result, research has shifted focus to model-based approaches that learn an environment's transition model to make more informed decisions. Although these methods are more data-efficient in simulations, real-world applications continue to pose challenges. A new strategy has been introduced that combines an induction rule set with logic-based supervision to create a more efficient learning pipeline. Specifically, this method utilizes Inductive Logic Programming to learn an transition rule set initially, which is then utilized to train a transition model. Following this, a version of the LSTMs' attention mechanism, termed as FocusNet, is used to model the dynamics of the environment. In experiments, this approach has been applied to real-world data from an industrial robotic system, which suggests that a more general and extensible method for robotic state transitions could be developed.

We investigate a specific type of non-equilibrium phononic fluid, characterized by a short optical path difference and unequal optical reflectivity, and demonstrate its capability of producing squeezed states in the optical spectrum, with corresponding applications in linear image stabilization and optical sensing technologies.

Our research addresses a functional minimax problem as part of a broader investigation into Fenton type minimax problems. The problem in focus seeks to find the minimal maximal value of the sum of translates of continuous functions on a compact group K, subject to certain positivity constraints. To approach this, we first establish a straightforward two-sided inequality for the sum of translates of continuous functions on a compact group K. Then, by applying a technique of differentiation, we derive a dual inequality that provides an upper bound for this sum. The application of Riesz' representation theorem to the underlying functional on K enables us to resolve the Fenton type minimax issue in a practical manner. In addition, by exploring connections with Gelfand pairs and regular Gelfand pairs, we are able to determine the exact values of the sum of translates of continuous functions on these pairs under specific positivity constraints. The result of Cossigra, Ganguly and Sengupta on the exact sum of translates of continuous functions on a regular Gelfand pair also finds verification in this study. The case of the symmetric group S3 is considered as a numerical example to illustrate the findings of the study.

Research on the shadow-world hypothesis, primarily focusing on its gravity and interactions related to Liouville's theorems, has been presented in recent studies. An assumption was made regarding how matter is affected by this shadow world, with some claims supported by Liouville's theorems but others requiring additional validation. We examine the possibility of spin-dependent interactions between the visible and shadow worlds, an idea not previously explored in those studies. By introducing a new framework incorporating Liouville's theorems, we set out to discover whether spin-dependent interactions could mediate a measurable attractive force between two electrons, as observed in experiments with $^6$Li. Our findings demonstrate that, depending on various parameters such as the mass of the shadow electrons and their Liouville equations, spin-dependent interactions alone can explain the experimental results, an outcome not solely attributable to electrostatic forces between electrons. This serves to further constrain the parameters in the modified Liouville equations, a crucial aspect of the theoretical framework.

Blind image restoration, encompassing deblurring, denoise, and dering, are key image enhancement problems having significant implications in various real-world contexts. These problems are distinguished by their underlying observation models, which are unknown and inaccessible in the case of blind scenarios. To overcome this limitation, we propose an innovative solution that establishes a lower boundary for the l1 approximation error using kernel mixture models. By formulating these models as convex optimization problems, we develop techniques to increase model complexity and reduce the error to any desired magnitude. We apply this framework to the solution of three key blind restoration problems, namely deblurring, denoise, and dering, and present the most advanced version as a new method called Blind Channel Estimation via Kernel Mixture (BCE-KM). To demonstrate its effectiveness, we show the results of applying this method to the well-known Blind Deblurring via Intensity-Source Model (BID-ISM) problem, and our findings indicate that it outperforms the current benchmark approach in all aspects. To facilitate the practical use of our method, we provide the necessary code and pre-trained models at the location of https://github.com/Deep-Logic/BCE_KM/tree/main/main.

This paper introduces a new concept called nonuniform associative Yang-Baxter equations from a coordinate-free perspective. These evolution equations have multiple applications, including the development of nonuniform multi-component vector continued fraction expansion and the formal power series method for solving partial differential equations.

Formal verification using Hoare logic offers a sound approach to validating the correct operation of programs by relating their input/output behavior to logical descriptions of a program's intended functionality. This methodology, while thoroughly established in academia, faces a significant limitation in its practical application to real-world software development due to its labor-intensive nature and the high level of mathematical expertise required. This difficulty is compounded by the fact that many software systems, including artificial intelligence programs, are designed in a high-level, abstract manner and only later translated into a lower-level form that is amenable to Hoare logic. In order to overcome this challenge, we have devised a novel approach that is grounded in the semantic relationship between natural language descriptions of a program's behavior and the logical forms representing that description. This approach, referred to as Natural Hoare Logic, is an advancement that is independent of the specific mathematical framework in use and is focused on the translation process of a program from an abstract, high-level description to its final implementation form. The goal of this methodology is to verify that the translation of an original natural language description and its corresponding low-level implementation are in agreement. If this verification is successfully accomplished, it provides formal confirmation that the implementation accurately captures the original natural language specification. This description and implementation are collectively known as dual specifications. In this study, we have demonstrated the efficacy of Natural Hoare Logic through a practical verification of a dual specification, accurately modeling a classical reasoning task for a cognitive system, as described using description logics.

Distributed consensus among heterogeneous processes is the foundation for reliable data storage, as illustrated by distributed database systems such as Amazon Dynamo and LevelDB. The Canopus algorithm achieves this consensus efficiently, with an O(D + H) round complexity, where D is the transmission delay and H is the hierarchy depth. The key innovation in Canopus is its ability to mitigate slow process interference through a quantitative approach to bounding slow process contributions. This paper presents RCanopus, a Canopus variant that is specifically designed to handle failures and malicious processes. The round complexity of RCanous is identical to Canopus, with a trade-off of increased message exchange, although it also provides stronger guarantees, as it is fault-tolerant in both the presence of failures and malicious processes.

Despite the essential role that cell membranes play in cellular functions, their physical properties, particularly those influenced by cholesterol, are still not fully understood. Due to its great impact on membrane functions, like signaling and fluidity, the presence of cholesterol has been a subject of much interest for centuries. Although several approaches have been used to study cholesterol's effects, such as using atomic force microscopy or making lipid pseudopeptides, these methods only provide limited insights into how cholesterol affects the mechanical properties of cell membranes. To gain a more comprehensive understanding of how cholesterol influences the flexural stiffness of cell membranes, researchers have developed a new method that utilizes a bilayer-blublet device. This method, also known as the BBD method, enables the direct measurement of the pressure-area curves, allowing the calculation of the flexural modulus of cell membranes and their models. This approach was verified in this study by measuring the flexural modulus of full-length phosphatidylcholine membranes and comparing it to that of model systems containing cholesterol. The results showed that the presence of cholesterol significantly increases the flexural modulus of the membranes. Moreover, by analyzing the pressure-area curves and calculating the radius of the molecules, researchers found that the increased flexural modulus resulting from the presence of cholesterol can be explained by the formation of ordered domains within the membranes. Using the BBD approach, this study provides the first direct measurement of the flexural modulus of cholesterol-containing model systems across the entire pressure-area curve.

We start by forming a composite system consisting of a star and black hole. Using the Arnowitt-Deurielt formalism, we convert the combined metric of the space surrounding the star into loop quantum gravity form. The resulting theory is applied to 1D and 2D cases, yielding models for the equations of state and behavior of the space in and around the star. A new metric is introduced which separates the gravitational field into the space around the star and inside the event horizon. A 2-parameter model is derived which predicts when and how the star transforms into a black hole.

Over the initial operation period of the Pierre Auger Observatory, which lasted for nearly two decades, researchers collected extensive data on ultra-high-energy cosmic rays, spanning more than 19 years of observation. During this period, 19 events were detected with energies exceeding 52 EeV and extremely precise arrival times, comparable to the width of the arrival times for proton-driven showers reaching 60 km away from the detector. Concurrently, an experiment at the Telescope Array yielded four similar events, with their combined data suggesting an isotropic distribution of ultra-high-energy cosmic particles, with their energy peaks potentially occurring around 52-53 EeV. With such findings, researchers rule out a dominant role for very high-energy galaxies producing such energetic particles and instead consider two main explanations: cosmic particles of light composition or magnetic field fluctuations during cosmic processes. An analysis with parametric representations of cosmic density across space also indicated that these energetic particles are uniformly distributed across the universe, with one representation suggesting a connection to the changes in cosmic structure at Z = 20-30, approximately 1 billion years ago. An alternative representation with 11 free parameters by Gavalec et al., which also described the data on relativistic cosmic particles at high and intermediate energies during the same period across the sky, with the exception of a small anisotropy in the local Virgo region, revealed that these energetic particles are uniformly distributed across the universe and suggested that these energetic particles are isotropic.

Incorporating deep neural networks into high-stakes applications like self-driving cars demands more precise uncertainty assessments for object classification and localization. Although some popular object detectors show confidence in their predictions, they often overstate their reliability. We present BayesOD, a method designed to generate more realistic uncertainty estimates for deep object detectors by reinterpreting the output distributions in an embedding-specific representation space, where the uncertainty is measured based on the standard deviation of the Gaussian posterior. By converting the output distributions of the anchor boxes in CornerNet into this representation, we obtain uncertainty values that can be utilized to derive an embedding space representation interpretable by humans. We perform experiments using CornerNet, DLA-CNN, and RetinaNet, both with and without the IoU-ranking loss on the MSD dataset, showcasing our method's ability to outperform existing uncertainty estimation methods in terms of uncertainty calibration and the correlation between uncertainty and classification accuracy. The code for BayesOD is available at https://github.com/ScriptingNinja/BayesOD.

Recent research on traffic forecasting has gained significant interest, driven by the potential for safety enhancements and route optimization. Unlike earlier studies, which focused on small spatial areas, recent advancements have leveraged larger-scale data, including multiple intersections. Building on this progress, our research leverages even larger contexts - 'traffic moving snippets' that include adjacent intersections and extends this scope temporally. To capitalize on this larger data, our method combines bidirectional long short-term memory and convolutional networks with attention. To mitigate the memory limitations associated with working with larger contexts, our approach utilizes a stacked attention mechanism that distributes attention weights more efficiently. Experimental validation on a high-resolution traffic dataset reveals that our method outperforms existing methods, utilizing relevant information without the need for manual selection or optimization of parameters.

In gray categories, we investigate revisions of gray categories, abelian gray categories, and preadditive gray categories. We establish a detailed analysis, including a general revision theorem. We explore specific cases in detail, particularly in gray categories. We use these results to investigate coherence in bi-, quasi-, and gray categories. Notably, we prove that in quasi-categories, every gray category is fully fully fully coherent if and only if it is monoidal. Additionally, we show that in 2-categories, every fully coherent gray category yields a coherent 2-category when equipped with a non-degenerate 2-dimension map.

The hippocampus is an essential brain region particularly vulnerable to damage caused by seizures and neurodegenerative diseases such as epilepsy and Alzheimer's disorder. Hippocampus segmentation in 3D imaging data is a critical aspect of research in these conditions, but manually segmenting it is a time-consuming and challenging task even for experienced neuroanatomists. Automated segmentation using convolutional neural networks is a promising alternative that has been largely underutilized and studied individually, despite their potential benefits. This research leverages four previously trained convolutional networks - ART, DeepLabv3+, U-Net, and ResNet - to analyze and compare their performance in segmenting hippocampi from epilepsy and Alzheimer's patients. Our findings reveal that hippocampi from patients with epilepsy can be accurately identified (87.11% +/− 2.00%), but those with Alzheimer's were less accurately segmented (80.91% +/− 3.10%). When evaluating the convolutional networks' ability to solve this task, ResNet emerged as the top performer with Art and DeepLabv3+ close runners-up, demonstrating the potential of these methods to contribute significantly to future research in hippocampu-based imaging studies for epilepsy and Alzheimer's disorder.

We investigated two-dimensional simulates of Bell's theorem using macroscopic techniques with visible lights and discovered that applying the pigeonhole principle to transverse light patterns allowed us to efficiently identify the outcomes of all interactions between particles without scaling accordingly. This approached proven to be equivalent to Bell's non-locality, which we experimentally validated through two macroscopic experiments performed over nearly eight hours. Both experiments involved recording the long-term average value of linked transversal light patterns, which exhibited non-local properties and the ability to efficiently describe multiple interactions outcomes without scaling. This finding confirmed the pigeonhole phenomenon as a highly effective mechanism for describing non-locality, even in complex macroscopic systems.

Our analysis investigates the contribution of cosmic ray albedo neutron decay (CRAND) to the trapped proton and alpha populations in Earth's orbit at geosynchronous altitudes, taking into account their simultaneous trapping mechanisms. To assess the accuracy of previous predictions, we conducted a Monte Carlo simulation for these particles, considering all relevant interactions up to a few hundred GeV/c. Our simulation shows that, in this energy range, particles trapped in opposite magnetic poles have equal concentrations of proton and alpha particles, resulting in an overestimation of the total particle population by a factor related to the ratio of albedo to primary cosmic ray densities. Our simulation reproduces the in situ measurements of this particle population and provides an alternative explanation for the observed trapped particle density being 40% higher than predicted without considering CRAND. Additionally, we found that, in this model, the total trapped particle population is dominated by contributed particles rather than albedo particles, with the latter accounting for only 1-13% of the total population in the 0.1-300 GeV/c region. Our results demonstrate the validity of previous CRAND-related research and offer a quantitative understanding of trapped particle densities in this model.

A comprehensive framework called Deep GNNs Framework is proposed, which underpins a wide range of GNN-based models with dynamic skeletons and adaptive topologies. The proposed framework is rooted in a novel interpretation of the global pyramid-like shrinkage skeleton paradigm. It uncovers two implicit assumptions inherent to typical pyramid-based models: the assumption of linear progression and limited neighbourhood knowledge. Both assumptions are found to be flawed. A linear progression is impractical due to the inherent characteristics of GNNs, while limited neighbourhood knowledge may hinder the effective global communication of valuable information. To address these shortcomings, a new framework is designed, which incorporates a novel progression mechanism and taps into neighbourhood knowledge at each stage. Furthermore, a local reconfiguration strategy is developed, which dynamically optimizes network links to refine node representations. The proposed framework is versatile, as evidenced by its rigorous theoretical analysis, extensive corroboration of expressive power, its generalisable and parameter-efficient design that effectively integrates neighbourhood knowledge and reconfigures links, and successful applications on diverse node classification and link prediction tasks, which yield superior results over baseline models and a recently proposed powerful method.

The objective of differential privacy is to safeguard confidential data while sharing insights obtained from incomplete data sets. Low-rank matrix completion, crucial for private data analytics, poses an intriguing problem as providing differential privacy for existing methods is highly challenging. Although various privacy protection methods, such as noise addition and quantization, have been explored, completing a matrix in a privately feasible manner remains an unresolved issue. Given the rapid advancement of machine learning and data analysis, developing innovative low-rank matrix completion methods with differential privacy that are both efficient and theoretically justifiable is essential. This study proposes a novel, quantization-based approach to matrix completion, incorporating differential privacy, and provides mathematical proofs for its accuracy and privacy. The results demonstrate how varying the quantization range affects the trade-off between information retention and structural consistency in the matrix. Furthermore, experimental findings indicate that our method outperforms existing, non-quantization based private matrix completion approaches.

We propose a novel approach to describe interstellar dust where larger grains are comprised of a uniform material, known as astrodust, and tiny particles, known as PAHs, are formed through a variety of processes including dust destruction and agglomeration. Our model highlights the significance of a background grain population in determining the overall dust properties and points out inconsistencies between existing data and theoretical models regarding dust polarization properties. This model is then used to investigate and explain the unknown aspects of dust destruction, agglomeration, and growth, and to analyze the impact of a typical interstellar dust mixture on the optical, polarized, and total extinction properties. This analysis concludes by offering suggestions for future observations and experiments to refine our understanding of interstellar dust.

Research on low-mass stars in the lower Taurus region allowed a global analysis 
of circumstellar disks using millimeter-wave interferometry. This included the 
analysis of temperature variations and gas-to-dust ratios in the disks. CIDA-1 
was specifically examined due to an anomalous light curve that suggested a massive 
planet, and also its unusually high gas-to-dust ratio compared to other disks. 
Using a radiative transfer code to simulate CIDA-1's disk, the results showed that 
the gas-to-dust ratio, at 1000:1, was significantly higher than the typical 50:1 
and 100:1 for other disks with and without planets, respectively. This indicated 
that the gas in CIDA-1's disk was significantly reduced by the presence of a 
planet. Two solutions were able to adequately explain CIDA-1's disk's thermal 
emissions and CO snow line locations: one involved a planet with 10 Jupiter-mass 
located at 8 stellar radii, and another with a 5 Jupiter-mass located at 5.5 
stellar radii, in conjunction with a binary system not far from it. However, it's 
not clear if these planets explain CIDA-1's disk's excessive gas through planet 
evolution. This study's findings show that in the case of CIDA-1's disk, massive

The study of the Lights Out problem on cycles has been carried out, with a specific tap count optimal solution found for n tap cycles with n being a multiple of 4 plus 1. Furthermore, an optimal solution for n tap cycles with n being a multiple of 4 has also been derived. Additionally, exact tap counts were obtained for a number of specific cycles, including those of lengths 7, 13, 21, and 31. An algorithm for constructing an optimal sequence of taps was designed, and from it, a most taps problem on cycles was developed. This algorithm was then extended to investigate the Lights Out problem on two-way cycles, resulting in a formula for calculating an optimal sequence of taps. This formula was then utilized to investigate a most taps problem on two-way cycles, with specific optimal tap counts calculated for a number of specific even N, including 7, 13, 21, and 31.

This study introduces a novel variational image segmentation model integrated with image restoration results, leveraging a detailed statistical representation of class priors through mixtures of Gaussian distributions. The model is trained on the challenging COCO-SEG 157 dataset, comprising 157 images with ground truth segmentations, along with the BSDS500 dataset for training Gaussian priors. We conduct comprehensive evaluations on the PASCAL VOC 2010 development set and the PASCAL Challenges benchmark, showcasing the model's exceptional performance in edge detection and image segmentation. Furthermore, the model demonstrates impressive segmentation results very close to the original input image quality due to its integration with an image reconstruction component, using either data-driven or variational statistical priors for noise removal. These findings illustrate that robust edge detection and segmentation can be achieved through the analysis of noisy images, enhancing statistical models of edge priors in the process.

The precision of abstract interpretation can be enhanced over standard techniques implemented in most tools, but often comes at a cost precluding its use in everyday settings. We propose a new approach, dubbed "descent from precision," incorporating recently discovered abstract representations, thereby enabling precision upgrades without initial precision settings. The underlying mathematics involves combining abelian and nonabelian semigroups, along with considerations for intersection, union, and overlapping computations in abstract domains, all of which are addressed in the accompanying paper's sections.

A broad range of structural, thermal, and electrical properties can be controlled
through the application of light in perovskite oxides due to their ion variability.
This versatility allows changing the topology of phonons by laser irradiation
atroom temperature, which has been demonstrated experimentally and theoretically.
Results show that phonons in perovskite oxides exhibit topological transformations
induced by laser light, which can be utilized to manipulate thermal conductivity
and regulate charge transport through the use of photonic devices. Furthermore,
these photonic effects may significantly influence the functionality and durability
of perovskite optoelectronic devices used in various applications.

Unsupervised outlier detection in various fields including data mining, databases, and machine learning relies heavily on distance-based methods in metric spaces. Recent work proposes the PROXY graph for this purpose, leveraging pseudo-distance metrics to improve detection. However, the underlying methods in PROXY are prone to high computational and memory demands. To solve this, a more efficient and scalable variant of the PROXY graph, known as the Lightweight PROXY graph, or LPROXY, is introduced. LPROXY reduces the complexity of its methods while retaining the OUTLIER score's accuracy, resulting in faster detection times and lower memory usage. LPROXY achieves this through two optimizations: combining method steps and utilizing more efficient data structures. On real-world datasets, LPROXY has shown significant performance improvements over the original PROXY, returning detection results an average of 40.0% and 84.3% faster, and requiring 65.1% and 85.6% less memory, respectively.

The interaction between an atom moving rapidly towards a mirror has the capacity to both induce stimulation of emission in other atoms within the system and lead to the scattering of electromagnetic radiation from the moving atom, phenomena which can only occur when the atom is moving towards a stationary state that it occupies at a standstill. By exploring this atom-mirror setup with an input of a two-level system as the moving atom, it's discovered that radiation emitted from the atom due to stimulation, in addition to initial and repeated rounds of absorption and emission, bears a distinct pattern resembling a logarithmic progression, indicating a decrease in intensity as the atom approaches the mirror, decelerating towards a stationary state where emission eventually ceases at the mirror's surface boundary. Conversely, when the atom is in motion away from the mirror towards a higher energy state it's in a state of excitation in a stationary position, a scenario in which repeated and periodic radiation emission and scattering occurs due to gaps in energy, only to reaccelerate as the atom moves further away from the mirror, culminating in an increase in intensity as the atom moves increasingly further from the mirror, decelerating towards a plateau where the intensity of emission gradually approaches an asymptotic state. Moreover, it's found that within a specific parameter range defined by a phase, on one hand a phenomenon of spontaneous emission is observed, while on the other hand a phenomenon of stimulated emission prevails. Recovering community structure from large network data is challenging, particularly when it comes to extremely complex networks. Standard tools, like spectral methods, are not effective for these networks due to their reliance on a specific dimensionality (λ). Additionally, existing fairness concerns in graph clustering tend to focus on overall group and node properties, thus overlooking a crucial aspect of community fairness - local integrity. This paper introduces a new framework that addresses these limitations by incorporating a global fairness constraint using a leader-following approach and a local consistency constraint within each community. Specifically, we formulate a variable λ that adapts to the specific graph, and key to this framework is the specification of 'neighborhood' as a localized fair representation. Through our framework, we demonstrate improved community structure, unbiased group assignment, and adjusted λ values, all of which are fully optimized, explained, and empirically validated using various real-world datasets.

This research focuses on kinetic models for reversible enzyme reactions, describing the dynamics of reactants and products using Markov transition kernels on a state space that includes all possible enzyme states. The paper assesses the effectiveness of two simple numerical integration methods, evaluating their ability to approximate exact iterative solutions of the kinetic equations. The analysis also explores the rate at which these approximations converge to the exact solution, considering both finite and limiting time intervals.

A study involving 13 TeV proton-proton collisions was conducted, utilizing data collected by the CMS experiment and spanning approximately 37 inverse femtobarns of luminosity. The research focused on identifying supersymmetric particles by examining final states featuring at least one jet and greater than 250 GeV of transverse momentum missing in the collision. Combining numerous simplified models of supersymmetric particle collisions, the CMS experiment presented a search for diverse supersymmetric particle masses using advanced kinematical variables and machine learning tools. Based on this analysis, the CMS experiment ruled out specific supersymmetric scenarios including: the production of 1.4 TeV gluino pairs accompanied by 0.8 TeV neutralino production and the production of 1.3 TeV top squark pairs accompanied by 0.7 TeV neutralino production, assuming the lightest supersymmetric particle mass was minimal. The CMS experiment further constrained the cross sectional probabilities for these diverse supersymmetric scenarios providing additional bounds on the mass spectrum of supersymmetric particles.

We examined three distinct expectations models, each accounting for varying levels of financial crisis severity and information dissemination delays. These include the traditional mean-reverting model as proposed by Diba and Startz (1987), the "black swan" model developed by Benhabil et al. (2011) with a unit root expectation process, and a model indicating the expectation process begins with perturbations in a unit root process only when the bubble commences. A computational analysis revealed that the initial model is unable to detect bubbles, while the later models are capable of identifying bubbles in financial asset pricing. Furthermore, our analysis suggests that asset prices may maintain positivity due to convexity even in models indicating mean-reverting price dynamics. We presented actual financial data examples that indicate that assets subject to rational expectations bubbles can experience significantly higher volatility during normal times and incur substantial losses during financial crises.

Quantum harmonic oscillators that evolve under periodic driving forces are studied using a novel approach that adapts coherent states for sampling. We've developed a detailed calculation for expecting a particle to be located at various positions during the cycle. This expectation involves summing coherent states located at different potential minima, weighted by their statistical significance. We've used a Markov Chain Monte Carlo method to derive an expression resembling a classical fractal, which diverges from another recent outcome due to a difference in state sampling. We've also explored the time-dependent expectation of a position classical-like variable, finding it differs significantly from the corresponding classical outcome when the driving force is strong.

Recent research has shown significant progress in enhancing online shopping experiences through item recommendation systems. These advancements aim to address various challenges posed by the diverse nature of data and rapidly changing user preferences over time. One key difficulty arises from the inherent subjectivity of human sentiment and emotions, giving rise to review bias. This study tackles this issue from a review-centric perspective, bringing together both reviewer and product information to create a cohesive, adaptable system. Our proposed Sentiment-aware Interactive Fusion Network (SIFN) achieves this by utilizing reviewer sentiment patterns to refine recommended products. To accomplish this, SIFN models complex reviewer behaviors and integrates a sentiment-aware module to synthesize reviewer characteristics. When paired with item features, this system provides a comprehensive view of reviewer characteristics and relevant items. An interactive module then fine-tunes these representations by focusing on shared, commonalities and differences between reviewers and individual items. Extensive experiments validate the effectiveness of SIFN, demonstrating improved performance and a clearer understanding of reviewer characteristics and recommended items.

Developing CS datasets is crucial to overcome Arab world's balancing act between two languages. A new approach utilizing Lexical Substitution to enhance data augmentation in CS is presented. This will especially benefit low-resource CS configurations by increasing dataset size. We examined four different LS algorithms: Sequential, Conditional, Joint, and Mutual Information-based. By applying these algorithms to the SECL dataset, we discovered that only the Conditional method efficiently creates switched samples and significantly improves the model's performance. Experiments were also conducted on the Arabic-English CS data set, which showed that combining the original and augmented data leads to better results in the Conditional setting.
