This research develops a novel variant of the fuzzy k-means (FKM) algorithm, tailored to handle high-dimensional data. The proposed approach captures local data characteristics by assigning different weights to features, based on their contribution to reconstruction error and measured indirectly through entropy values, which evaluate the feature's ability to pinpoint data points. The combination of weighted features with fuzzy clustering enables the clustering algorithm to incorporate both local neighborhood relationships and significant feature influences. The novel entropy-driven variable feature weighted fuzzy k-means (EVFWFM) algorithm has been tested on simulated and real-world datasets, comparing its performance to established state-of-the-art fuzzy clustering methods.

The Mixture-of-Experts model has been a cornerstone for parameterized function approximation due to its versatility and accuracy in modeling complex functions, yet it's known for being difficult to optimize efficiently. Researchers have particularly struggled with overcoming the challenges of varying training samples between sub-networks and the overall model. In an attempt to break through this barrier, we present a new algorithm that surpasses the current best results for Mixture-of-Experts by achieving a significantly faster and more efficient training process while maintaining improved accuracy. We achieve this breakthrough by leveraging a new method of sub-network training, where instead of being limited by a fixed number of data samples, the networks can be dynamically and efficiently trained to their optimal capacity. This innovation reveals a fundamental limitation in previous approaches and we demonstrate that our algorithm addresses this flaw directly, resulting in a notable enhancement of the model's capacity to learn from available data.

We primarily investigate a specific chip-firing game on the edges of the Mordell-Lefschetz puzzles, except when the fiber numbers are 2 or odd; in those cases, we also explore the complement. Initially, we identify the dual Jacobians of the covers associated with even fiber numbers and demonstrate they are isomorphic to a product of two Jacobians, one of which is the Jacobian of the curve itself, with the other being a Jacobian of a different genus. Following this, we categorize the types of these Jacobians into six distinct categories: Hurwitz, primitive, image, self-dual primitive, an extension of Mordell-Lefschetz, and a combination of both. Furthermore, we extend our analysis to include the Prym varieties of all these covers and show that each of their types can be described as either primitive, image-related, or derived from another. We also establish that the types of all covers can be enumerated using a specific list of minimal types, which we determine.

We examine the possibility of global symmetry breaking in quantum gravity on a cosmic scale, considering two main theories: the Templeton mechanism and the Charap Betti Louremann Street theory. According to the Templeton mechanism, global symmetries can be broken in our early universe due to interactions with dark matter, whereas the Charap Betti Louremann Street theory suggests that global symmetry breaking can be observed in the universe's large-scale irregularity. Investigations into the universe's refractive properties, as measured in experiments such as the Ptolemy experiment, have not uncovered any signs of symmetry breaking. Additionally, our analysis of the universe's large-scale patterns and refractive behavior has imposed strict limitations on the possible range of symmetry-breaking parameters.

Our  research, which utilized ultraviolet (UV) optical data from the Astronomical
Telescope's Ultraviolet Imaging Telescope (UVIT), examined the photometry of ten
bright stars in the globular cluster NGC 4147. By analyzing a B-V color vs. V-B
plot, we identified five blue stars and four red stars and two unclassified white
stars. Further investigation through the 2MASS J024531.36-482554.6 catalog confirmed
our initial classifications. Furthermore, we discovered that the red stars were not
burning hydrogen on their blue horizontal branch but instead were in various
stages of core helium burning. Additionally, we found a blue straggler mechanism
as a plausible explanation for the origin of the five blue stars. Also, we obtained
a first look at one newly discovered white star that required further follow-up
observations with the Gravitational wave local black hole instrument. Lastly, we
calculated the overall magnitude of NGC 4147 to be 5.774.

A key concept, known as the b-principle, revolutionizes problem-solving by converting combinatorial difficulties into geometric difficulties, thereby simplifying the issue. A revised version of the b-principle, referred to as the fragile b-principle, takes into account the errors, offering flexibility in the transfer of properties. This document provides an in-depth explanation of how the fragile b-principle applies to Thom's Mumford conjecture. Thom's conjecture posits that the mapping of a compact, orientable surface to the 2-sphere can be broken down into two separate mappings: one from a surface to a polytopal sphere and another from a polytopal sphere to the 2-sphere. Although the original statement is incorrect, as evidenced by the existence of highly irregular maps, a modified version of the conjecture can be proven using the fragile b-principle.

The transfer learning phenomenon remains largely misunderstood, and attempts to streamline it through visualizations have proven incomplete. This paper presents a more comprehensive and structurally sound conceptualization of transfer learning, dividing it into two distinct aspects - similarity and sufficient data availability. The first aspect encompasses cases where the training and testing datasets share semantic commonalities, whereas the second aspect involves scenarios where datasets differ significantly, yet the testing dataset comprises ample data. This dual-framework helps pinpoint the underlying causes of model failure and successful transfer learning outcomes, and it also reveals that success in one area does not necessarily guarantee it in the other. Experimental evaluations using various network architectures, training methods, and test-clustering configurations were conducted on MNIST, MNIST-SF, and EMNIST datasets to validate the proposed framework, and it was found that explicitly incorporating the sufficient data factor could enhance the model's performance in data-sparse yet semantically distinct scenarios.

In various scenarios, such as the spread of opinions or diseases, understanding the rate of information or entity spread within a network is crucial. Despite recognition of network structure influence, the impact of this structure is not consistently recognized. We investigated how the network's topology affects the rate of information or entity spread. We found that in all cases, the rate of spread is influenced by the network's connectivity and population distribution, specifically that which resides in highly connected areas. We determined the rate of spread in different scenarios by analyzing the network's cluster structure and how information or entities transition between these clusters. This led to the development of a speed spread framework, which incorporates key parameters: the network's cluster connectivity, boundary strength, and cluster size distribution. We validated this framework through numerical simulations and real-world applications, such as the spread of scientific knowledge or technological advancements. Furthermore, we discussed how our framework can help in the prediction and management of various phenomena, such as the spread of ideas or technological or biological dissemination.

Geometric quantifiers of regularity are necessary for classify solutions to partial differential equations, including PDEs involving analytic functions like the Monge-Ampere equation in complex geometry. In this context, a tool called quantitative measures on analytic sets is developed, which provides regularity estimates for the sets based on a given parameter. Fano manifolds, known for their complex geometry PDEs like the $(-1)$-Kahler form conjecture, are restricted in their application, with the quantitive measures on singularities playing a crucial role. Moreover, unique characteristics of Fano varieties, along with compactness, suggest that the conjecture has limitations in its broad applicability, particularly with the presence of torus actions, thus influencing results on degenerating Fano varieties like toric Fano varieties and singularities of cubic and quartic surfaces. In using these varieties as examples, the mathematical objectivity of the constructed measures is demonstrated, revealing relationship with existing geometric measures of regularity and the potential to accurate calculate any set based on analytic functions.

We propose a new discrete-time approach to analyze the regular perturbation model for unamplified quantum communication channels. These channels operate under non-uniform sampling patterns, which cannot be modelled accurately by conventional continuous-time methods that rely on regular perturbation theory. By examining the finite sampling rate of these channels, our framework provides an explicit expression for the precision of perturbation calculations, enabling characterization of the accuracy of these calculations at different sampling points. We validate the accuracy of our predictions by confirming they conform to established principles of consistency and causality. Furthermore, we apply our framework to a standard example of a channel that undergoes pair-splitting, deriving a precise formula for the logarithmic correction term that deviates from the leading perturbative result.

Android malware evasion attacks have become a significant concern for mobile security researchers. This type of attack circumvents detection by malicious apps, which can then proceed to inflict harm on mobile devices. Specifically, these attacks target specific parts of the Android system, namely app packaging and fingerprint creation. This study aligns with the definition of evasion attacks posed by Virgilio and colleagues in 2017 and provides an overview of these types of attacks within the Android framework.

Container orchestration tools such as Kubernetes and Mesos conventionally expect specific container formats like Docker, which limits users' ability to experiment with new container approaches. To address this, we introduce Ozy, a universal orchestration container designed from Kubernetes and Mesos' common features. By comparing Ozy with these established tools, we demonstrate that Ozy can replicate Kubernetes' scalability and Mesos' distributed capabilities while offering greater simplicity.

Our study utilizes a classical model to examine the statistical mechanics of a Landau-deformed Heisenberg model, particularly focusing on its behavior in a specific type of quantum insulator known as the fractional quantum Hall rest state. At moderate levels of Landau-level mixing, we discovered an unexpected phase at five-quarters filling that exhibits increased density variations. Contrary to traditional explanations of reentrant phases, this phenomenon occurs without the need for multiple competing interactions. Instead, it arises from a natural transition in the model's configuration at moderate mixing strengths, resulting in increased density fluctuations. We verified that these increased fluctuations could potentially explain recent numerical findings, and further, we suggest that this phase might be realized in experimental settings utilizing a specific type of fractional quantum Hall system known as the polarized spin-1 photoemitted electron system.

Our investigation examined the recently introduced Thakurta metric, proposed as a potential solution to the cosmological black hole problem from the perspective of gravitational wave physics. In particular, we investigated whether this model could be characterized as a frozen Fermi-Walker derivative system. By identifying key properties, we determined that the Thakurta metric is a Ricci soliton with a specific potential $\Phi=-\frac{1}{2}(ln)(\sqrt{-\Delta} + h.h.}, where h represents a spatially constant 3-dimensional matrix. However, our work reveals that a cosmological black hole's mathematical formulation relies on a specific form of the metric, specifically Einstein's gravitational field with a negative constant, nor can it be adequately represented by a 1+1 Riemannian manifold. Consequently, we conclude that the Thakurta metric is unlikely to be the best solution to the cosmological black hole problem. Additionally, we bound the density of primordial black holes using LIGO-Virgo data, establishing an upper limit of $KBH-\frac{20}{19}M_{\odot}h^{-2}h^{-1}h^{-1}h^{-0.5}h^{-0.25}h$.

The formation of protoplanets through pebble accretion is a critical process in how and when planets form. However, this process is often unclear especially in the early stages of how these pebbles are formed. A recent set of simulations explored how the presence of pebbles and small particles influence the formation of protoplanets and revealed that areas with high-density fluctuations play a significant role. Notably, in regions with significant density variations, large particles and pebbles concentrate in areas of low density and areas of high pressure respectively. This leads to a typical planetary formation pattern, whereas in uniform environments, this separation does not occur in a predictable sequence. Despite this, in uniform environments, planets composed primarily of silicate still form, even at very low densities. This challenges current theoretical models which assume that Saturnian-core formation occurs at much higher solid surface density environments. Finally, this work also supports the theory that gas giant cores are often formed through a combination of both core accretion and disk migration.

Many recent empirical findings regarding overparameterized models suggest that overparameterized models with sufficient data and a large enough sample size can achieve zero or low cross-validation errors despite their overly complex nature. However, these empirical results seem to contradict the theoretical predictions made by previous studies, indicating a significant gap between the existing theoretical frameworks and reality. This work aims to address this discrepancy by establishing that overparameterization can occur due to fundamental limitations in computation. By proving that accurate cross-validation, which is a standard evaluation metric in real-world applications, is not possible for overparameterized linear regression models under certain conditions, we can reconcile the existing empirical results with the theoretical predictions. This limitation also implies that overparameterization might not only apply to linear models but also extend to nonlinear regression models.

Three results were obtained; they build upon an earlier finding made by the first listed author, yet provide alternative evidence. In this current research, it was demonstrated that any given Bohr set found on an abelian group has an explicitly defined, arithmetic generating set. Additionally, it was observed that the set formed by the Bohr set's integers multiples, equaling the original set's measure as expected, was also formed. Lastly, it was concluded that the integer, n, the Bohr set measures, at n times the original measuring set, respectively n times the original measuring set, was also true, but only if n is positive and the original measuring set, was greater than or equal to, one eighth.

This study addresses the dial-a-ride problem within large urban settings where residents have one vehicle per household, and images is the number of cars per household. We develop a mixed-integer linear programming model and use branch-and-cut to find optimal solutions efficiently. Computational experiments were conducted with 213 instances from previous research under a 5-cars-per-household scenario, yielding a 0.04% gap in results, and these were compared to previous solutions, achieving 0.11% of the total costs could be improved.

We introduce an e-commerce pretraining model called Knowledge Understood Pretraining model for E-commerce shopping datasets (KUP-E) that utilizes mousereporting information and shopping query datasets containing vast amounts of unstructured product information. This knowledge includes how products are similar, comparisons between them, and attributes that define a particular product?  To tackle this, we develop a multi-modal encoder network that jointly learns the visual and language knowledge from the mouse data and shopping queries.  This KUP-E model differentiates itself from existing large language models by incorporating multi-modal learning, making it applicable for datasets outside of the general category due to its knowledge-driven approach?  To demonstrate its effectiveness, we apply the KUP-E model to several tasks such as product information completion, interactive question answering, and product grouping based on user behavior.  This KUP-E model significantly outperforms the current best-evaluation models and showcases robust performance on complex multi-modal datasets?  To our knowledge, this KUP-E model is the first to successfully apply large language models to various data sets beyond standard benchmarks?  This work highlights the efficacy of incorporating mouse data and corresponding driving queries for model pretraining?  This research opens a new avenue for developing more context-aware and knowledgeable models applicable to real-world datasets and complements the current trend of large language models?  This KUP-E model will be made available on the HuggingFace Model repository.

A significant characteristic of neurodegenerative diseases like Alzheimer's is the progressive deterioration of brain function. Since clinical diagnosis is typically made when significant damage has occurred, earlier detection through imaging and cognitive tests is crucial. However, effectively utilizing these methods to identify individuals at risk requires advanced methods of data analysis. This study proposes an approach grounded in a more comprehensive understanding of neuroscience to address the challenge of classifying normal control subjects and Alzheimer's patients based on magnetic resonance imaging and cognitive data. Specifically, the method employs Deep InfoMax, an extension of an advanced deep neural network, to extract a latent representation that maximizes information about class labels, thereby facilitating classification. However, an inherent limitation of this method is its difficulty in maintaining consistency between similar samples in the latent space, which can lead to a higher risk of overfitting. To address this, the dataset is augmented with a strategy called triple sampling, aimed at incorporating diversity and similarity among examples. Ultimately, the efficacy of this approach is demonstrated through an examination of data from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, with results revealing a substantial 93% classification accuracy for distinguishing normal controls and Alzheimer's patients, particularly when utilizing MR imaging alone.

In the context of understanding written text, advancements in natural language processing have primarily focused on incorporating the significance of word sequences and their interactions when constructing semantic representations. Nevertheless, existing methods still struggle to capture the intricate interactions within text content due to their limitations in computational efficiency and scope of applicability. Owing to the increasing role of word sequences in detecting interactions, a recurrent neural network is a natural fit for overcoming these limitations. Given that conventional interaction-based recurrent neural networks often neglect certain interactions that are hidden within the text, we propose an innovative, interaction-aware architecture that can effectively capture the complex, multi-layered interactions encoded within word sequences. The experimental outcomes confirm the superiority of the proposed model, demonstrating improved performance on both SICK-related tasks and the more demanding, SEMEval-based dataset that demands even greater sophistication.

In our investigation, we've enhanced the spin-orbit coupling in a two-orbital Hubbard model set in a honeycomb lattice, similar to those found in $\alpha$-RuSe and MoSe lattices. Our results from the mean-field approximation show that the critical value of spin-orbit coupling for transforming a metal to a spiral antiferromagnetic state is significantly lower than in graphene. Furthermore, we discovered that the critical value can be adjusted by modulating the interaction between identical orbitals. Moreover, through the self-consistent Hartree-Fock approach, we found that the spiral antiferromagnetic phase can be converted into an antiferromagnetic N\'eel phase by increasing the inter-orbital interaction.

We're investigating theories incorporating Shadow Matter, which can be modeled as a conformal field theory coupled with a conformal field theory carrying ghostly Noether charge. These two theories, individually long-established, have a combined model whose implications for a new class of spacetimes, specifically those with quantized negative mass, have yet to be explored. In this context, we're focusing on the action's variational properties rather than developing solutions for universal field equations. Our primary finding is that these new spacetimes possess a form of temporal and spatial self-similarity, which is further supported by the emergence of new symmetries within the shadow formalism. Consequently, we discover that the most substantial symmetry is the 2d conformal group, which remains unaltered when considering the additional 1/2 supersymmetry found in the simplest examples of the conformal tensor field theory.

To ensure that AI-powered medical devices function correctly in real-world scenarios, practitioners must assess their performance in diverse situations. Unlike the typical training-data setting, real-world scenarios can pose significant challenges, leading to a concept known as distribution shift occurring. Estimating an AI model's efficacy under such a shift is a major challenge in validating these medical devices. In this context, a new approach utilizing conformal prediction has been developed to provide reliable and accurate uncertainty quantification for classical model evaluation metrics. Furthermore, this method has been adapted to offer a more robust estimate of accuracy when training and testing datasets differ. We apply this approach to the problem of medical image analysis, specifically in labeling chest X-ray images with COVID-19 related symptoms, and validate it using a diverse dataset.

Highly ordered structures like DNA, proteins, and crystals require precise positioning of chemical groups, which is challenging in dynamic simulations. This issue arises because current algorithms don't adequately account for the extremely low probabilities of chaotic group arrangements in these systems. To address this limitation, we've developed a simple method for molecular dynamics simulations that involves setting chemical groups on a substrate like DNA, proteins, or crystals to a fixed state. This approach allows us to increase the occurrence rate of these arrangements in dynamic simulations, leading to more accurate results. We've confirmed the effectiveness of our technique by applying it to a simple DNA model, where we've shown that our method enables exploration of a wider range of DNA configurations than would be possible through random searches. This strategy is straightforward to use with existing MD programs and has the potential to significantly improve the simulation of very low probability chemical arrangements in biological systems.

Arithmetic-to-Entropy (ANS) is a widely used lossless data compression technique, renowned for its minimal side information requirements and straightforward implementation. At optimal compression, ANS mirrors the Shannon limit, albeit with reduced decoding speed. Despite its prevalence, the trade-off between compression ratio and decoding speed hasn't been extensively analyzed in existing studies. This paper seeks to fill this knowledge gap by investigating various ANS layer configurations through both theoretical calculations and simulations, highlighting the consequences of the ANS entropy encoding on compression performance. By identifying the most effective configuration, this study aims to illustrate Arithmetic Coding's influence on ANS's capabilities.

Knowledge of the dielectric properties of the pore solution is crucial in interpreting results from time-domain spectroscopy and modeling cement-based materials' moisture transport. However, due to cement paste's complex and non-equilibrium nature, the dielectric behavior exhibits both concentration- and frequency-dependent phenomena. To fill this gap, we investigated the dielectric properties of sodium nitrate solutions with concentrations mimicking those of fresh and mature pore solutions, spanning from 0.4 Mol/kg to approximately 5.5 Mol/kg. Our experiments covered a frequency range of 10^-2 to 10^3 Hz and temperatures from 10°C to 50°C, and we discovered a non-Arrhenius relationship governing the dielectric properties. We also found that, at temperatures above 30°C, the dielectric properties demonstrated a substantial temperature sensitivity. Furthermore, we observed a non-linear concentration-dependent dielectric behavior, particularly at lower frequencies, which transitioned into a more predictable Nernst-type relationship at higher frequencies. Our research offers a more accurate representation of cement paste's dielectric properties and enhances the simulation of pore solution dielectric properties, thereby contributing valuable insights for modeling cement-based materials' moisture transport and interpreting results from time-domain spectroscopy.

In this article, we examine the properties of heavy hadronic molecules, specifically focusing on X(3872), two kaons, and various charged and neutral P-wave states associated with the kaon-antikaon system, to determine if recent experimental findings of the BESIII collaboration support the existence of these molecules or if they can be interpreted as the hadronic decay products of excited resonances. Although the theoretical work presented here does not necessarily establish that all observed states are purely hadronic in nature, it does provide essential guidelines for future experimental studies, allowing us to identify which states can be confirmed as having a hadronic origin and which others must be dominated by a single resonance. The research findings presented here, combined with other results not discussed here, suggest that heavy hadronic molecules with a s-sbar component are likely real, while those without such a component are more difficult to verify. For example, the Y(4260) is primarily understood as being a $D^*D^*_{s0}(2317)$ molecule, whereas states like the $D^{(*)}D^{(*)}\bar{K}$ system exist only as $D^{*}(2317)$, which is then produced through the $D^*K$ mixing effect. On the other hand, the $D^{(*)}D^{(*)}$
and $\bar D^0\bar D^0\omega$ systems do not exist and are easily understood as being dominated by a single resonance

The escalating complexity of modern military conflicts is driving a need for increased efficiency, versatility, and adaptability in warfare tactics. This demand is particularly evident in critical areas like search-and-rescue operations, where swift decision-making and resource allocation are essential for survival. Unmanned systems have the potential to revolutionize these processes, and swarm technologies are likely to play a crucial role. By leveraging the power of language, we conducted a large-scale analysis of 181,000 scientific publications related to unmanned systems, allowing us to identify the key factors that influence their development. Notably, we found that the critical mass for funding and technological support for an unmanned system development corresponds to approximately $2 billion to $5 billion, beyond which the rate of progress accelerates exponentially. This insight enables us to pinpoint the specific areas where additional resources are likely to yield substantial gains in performance, efficiency, and resilience. From our results, we can conclude that the development of unmanned systems is heavily influenced by a limited number of key factors, including defense spending, number of employees in the relevant sector, and associated acronyms, as well as the rate of published research and related education institutions. Furthermore, we define and categorize various types of unmanned systems based on their intended application and stratify the influential factors within these groups, enabling us to better allocate resources and guidance for realization.

New simulations conducted at two distinct resolations, with and without hydrodynamic modeling, have been carried out to map the average properties of fluctuations in the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest across the line-of-sight across over 100,000 Hubble volumes. At the lower resolution (0.1 comoving Mpc) these simulations encompass the influence of primordial non-linearities, but not those produced by hydrodynamics. They also have an associated "pseudo-spectra' generated from the initial conditions used in the simulations. Combining the pseudo-spectra with the simulated spectra allows for a highly constrained model of the simulations' redshift-dependent mean flux. When we calculate a measure of correlation, cross-correlating these simulated spectra at different distances along the line-of-sight, we find that it closely resembles that of observed data, after it has been normalized. Furthermore, by utilizing the simulations we have constructed a highly constrained model of the simulations' redshift, cross-correlated flux autocovariance which shows a definite decrease in the fluctuations amplitude as redshift increases. When we compare this to the simulations and observed data, we find that it closely resembles that of observed data, after it has been normalized. By using the simulations to determine the average flux, we have calculated a cosmological constraint on the amplitude of fluctuations in the simulations, with a value of $1.0\pm 0.1$ and this constraint is at parity with the Lyman-$\

Researchers at Fermilab have successfully conducted an experiment where horizontal and vertical beam emittances were intentionally exchanged within a 66-meV proton beam. The experiment utilized a specially designed emittance exchange beamline, featuring two identical arc beams, within a warm beam test facility. The exchange was achieved through a plasma-based mechanism, facilitated by electron beam ionization of a gas pulsed cell containing argon. The study demonstrated the feasibility of emittance exchange for future intense pulsed beam applications and revealed that only the first pass through the pulsed cell contributed to emittance exchange, with approximately 66% efficiency, while beam losses due to the cell were kept below 2%.

A crucial capability for thousands of robots worldwide is automatic trajectory prediction. The predicted trajectories, however, lack diversity and accuracy due to limitations in current models, which typically rely on fixed sets of social indexing frameworks. As a result, these models fail to capture dynamic relationships between entities, resulting in a significant loss in trajectory diversity and accuracy. To address this limitation, this research proposes Sliding Sequential CVAE (SS-CVAE), an innovative method for trajectory prediction that incorporates a new time-variant socially-aware reevaluation mechanism. SS-CVAE generates predictions by first using a conventional sliding CNN to extract a dynamic representation of past agent interactions, which is then divided into past and current frames. A past-cnn encoder and a past-cnn social indexing framework are developed to encode past interactions, and to estimate current interactions and future agent goals, respectively. Furthermore, SS-CVAE incorporates a socially-aware reevaluation mechanism that allows it to reassess interactions based on the state of past interactions. Experimental evaluations of SS-CVAE demonstrate its exceptional performance on two datasets. SS-CVAE achieves significant improvements in diversity and accuracy compared to other advanced trajectory prediction methods, including Multi-Agent Trajectory Prediction with Factories of Features (MaF2CF) and Reinforcement Trajectory Prediction (R3DP). The project's code can be found at: https://github.com/whaiwhai/SS-CVAE.

This study examines information-based complexity measures in the context of basic Boolean networks, specifically Boltzmann Machines. It focuses on three such measures: Markov, conditional, and relative entropy complexity, in the realm of Boltzmann Machines with fully connected, undirected networks. The aim is to understand how these measures align with the system's parameters and to assess their correlations over varying configurations of the network. Findings indicate that all three measures show similar responses to parameter variations and that the measures often exhibit significant correlations despite their differences in magnitude. These results suggest that diverse information-based complexity measures offer complementary insights into Boolean networks, shedding light on their structural and functional properties. It is hoped that this work will lay the groundwork for further investigations into the characteristics of Boolean networks using complex measures.

This paper showcases initial hand signal detection results for swarm robotics applications using Long-Range Wide Area Network (LoRaNetwork). The LoRaNetwork enables the LoRa-enabled robots to recognize specific hand gestures from the human observer, facilitating a new type of interaction between humans and swarms of robots via the internet. The hand gesture data collected includes six unique movements (stop, left, right, rotate, double-left, and double-right), and experiments were conducted to assess the effectiveness of Long-Range Wide Area Network (LR-WAN) based hand gesture recognition. The analysis found that the accuracy of the LoRaNetwork's hand gesture recognition was 66% when the observer performed two consecutive actions, and 33% accuracy when the observer performed individual actions. These findings will serve as a foundation for enhancing the accuracy of the LoRaNetwork's hand gesture recognition in real-world applications.

The study aims to enhance the accuracy of white/basilar blood cell classification, an image classification task. We've taken two steps to improve the process: merged ensemble learning to combine the outputs of multiple neural networks, training with augmented images to increase model diversity, and utilizing Mitchell's mitosis annotation dataset for supervised learning. We've outdone the current standard dataset by introducing a comprehensive benchmark for annotated datasets.

A key advantage of counterdiabatic protocols in driving quantum states involves the use of a supporting, or supporting-like gauge potential. This potential has been shown to be present in all driving methods that maintain system ground-state quantum coherence. A variational approach can be employed to determine the driving mechanism, encompassing nonadiabatic techniques, which we apply specifically to the Hubbard model for creating initial ground states. By experimentally simulating the dynamics in the laboratory, we find that the gauge potential's magnitude is closely related to the rate of driving and the coupling between lattice sites, with strong interactions leading to significant potential. At the rate of exponential decay, the gauge potential's magnitude scales with this rate of driving and exhibits nonlinear dependence on the coupling between lattice sites within a certain range. A variation of the Hubbard model that includes an inhomogeneous magnetic field displays more complex behavior, with the gauge potential's magnitude fluctuations diminishing as the number of sites in the system increases.

This empirical color model transforms input RGB data into an extended RGB color space, where each component varies dynamically across a specified input range. Specifically, this component is used to control color shifts in technologies such as LCD and LED displays. We present a unique approach to high-dynamic range (HDR) tone mapping, an industry-standard process used to mitigate display constraints like a limited color gamut and color banding. We effectively combine HDR and LCD-friendly properties with HDR's dynamic range, resulting in an HDR-like image suitable for LCD displays. Due to its simple, efficient structure, this color model is compatible with most HDR tone mapping techniques. We have successfully integrated it into a few methods, yielding impressive outcomes. We have included HDR-like results using the JET tone mapping algorithm and a newly developed, efficient Yang's HDR tone mapping method in this research. Moreover, this color model can be used as a layer-independent color gradient map, suitable for interactive high-dynamic range (HDR) visualization. We have obtained excellent interactions with Yang's HDR and JET tone mapping methods, resulting in a higher range of Yang's HDR (1.6) and JET (1.6) and a more than 2-fold improvement in Yang's HDR and nearly a 3-fold improvement in JET tone mapping times.

The process of expanding a function in a series, known as a Taylor expansion, is critical and widely used in numerous applications. However, when a function is exponentially increasing, the traditional polynomial-type Taylor expansion is insufficient. We must employ Taylor-like expansions that can capture the function's rapidly changing behavior by using rational exponents. These types of expansions are essential for analyzing the dominant terms in highly nonlinear functions, including those that appear in higher-order renormalization group equations. We provide an alternative derivation of these exponentially increasing Taylor expansions using a technique called differential equations. We also derive a new set of formulas for inverse functions that generalize the conventional Taylor and inverse Taylor expansions.

Given a surface S equipped with a metric d, such that it meets the conditions set by Alexandrov for an upper curvature bound, this thesis investigates how covering maps harmonic on S relate to its uniformization into a sphere S^m, a smooth, m-dimensional sphere. Specifically, it identifies key criteria under which a covering map is harmonic if it meets certain structural conditions, and uses this to establish that any smooth, curved surface S meeting these conditions can be transformed into a sphere S^m without disrupting its essential structure.

A novel method for generating photon-photon physics can be formed by utilizing the interaction of laser-generated plasma waves with pairs of relativistic electrons produced by the interaction of a laser with a focalized seed field of its own frequency or a nearby, co-propagated oscillator field. This electron pairs are then subjected to the intense laser field, resulting in the production of pairs of high-energy particles that can subsequently undergo relativistic Collin-Bizzi or Chudakov pair annihilation in the intense laser field, thereby generating an energetic, collimated photon with energies up to a few hundred MeV. This approach offers several potential advantages, including a reduced requirement for seed field power, increased operational time, and the capability to generate photons with energies that are difficult to produce using the current state of laser technology. As an example of this concept, a simulation demonstrates the generation of photons with approximately 240 MeV of energy within an extremely small time frame and a minuscule volume, with a density of photons of approximately one kiloelectronvolt per steradian.

Introducing a second $Z_2$ symmetry alongside the standard model is a straightforward approach to modelize the breaking of $Z_2$ symmetry in the two Higgs doublet model. This model comes with a number of essential features such as a goldstino with a non-zero $A$-term and a dark matter particle which is stable due to a residual $Z_2$ symmetry. In this model, the mass of the dark matter particle, the Higgs vacuum expectation values, and the mixing between the two Higgs fields are all closely related to the softly broken $Z_2$ parameter, $m_{12}$. In this study, we examine how these parameters change in response to variations in the value of $m_{12}$. Our research focuses on two types of two Higgs doublet models: an extension of the standard model itself, and a more general model with discrete symmetry. Our results, obtained numerically, are based on the conditions under which dark matter is stable, and non-relativistic annihilation of dark matter is feasible.

Shape Expression schemas serve as comprehensive definitions for RDF data formats, encompassing constraints on data validity and normalization. Due to their rigor, Shape Expression schemas can unambiguously detail data formats, including hierarchical structures and constraints, such as uniqueness and cardinality. These comprehensive schema details can be utilized in various tasks like data validation, normalization, and compatibility checking. One significant application of Shape Expression schemas involves transferring data between different systems. In this context, we focus on conveying a Relational-to-RDF dataset as specified in an RDF schema (RDFS) using Shape Expression, but this task becomes complicated due to inherent limitations in Relational databases and the need to interpret optional and cardinality constraints defined by Shape Expression. To resolve these challenges, we have devised innovative solutions that ensure the compatibility and integrity of the conveyed dataset. We have also conducted experiments to evaluate different approaches for enhancing data consistency and explored the performance of our methods.

A significant number of applications in economics and computer science can be addressed using data enveloping, a method for observing high-level system performance using limited observational data. In recent years, computing power has enabled the processing of large datasets, while advances in optimization techniques have made way for the use of complex models in this field. Our open-source PyStoNED library provides an easy-to-use tool for applying various types of convex regression and non-differentiable optimization techniques, leveraging the capabilities of Scipy to handle complex models as needed.

In this research, we perform an in-depth analysis of semi-leptonic $t \bar t \phi$ production at the LHC using the latest combined results of the CMS and ATLAS detectors for setting direct limits on the 125 GeV Higgs boson's interaction with top quarks and the Higgs itself. We investigate various scenarios including fully hadronic, semi-leptonic, and fully leptonic detection methods. Additionally, we examine how these constraints would be affected by different event reconstruction techniques. Our study reveals that a more accurate determination of $\phi$-related events can be achieved through techniques that improve resolution on the $\tau$-jet identification and missing energy. This more accurate reconstruction also enables better distinction between the Higgs boson decay into $\tau \bar \tau$ and $\b \bar b$. On the other hand, missing energy reconstruction methods have less impact on distinguishing between these two decay channels. Furthermore, in certain situations where missing energy reweighting is applicable, it leads to a significant improvement in setting limits on top quark-$\phi$ coupling constraints. It is worth noting that incorporating $\phi$-related events detected via the missing energy will lead to a small reduction in Drell-Yan noise in hadronic decays. However, this effect depends on the specific phase space in question.

Recent advancements in natural language processing have led to significant improvements in language understanding through the use of pre-trained language models. These models, however, have traditionally been fine-tuned using supervised learning techniques. New developments are now focusing on using these models in unsupervised and few-shot learning methods. These approaches, inspired by semi-supervised learning and meta-learning, aims to significantly reduce the need for labeled data. Although some experiments have demonstrated the feasibility of leveraging large language models for these tasks, they have been conducted using experiment-specific models, thus restricting the scope of application. To expand on these findings, this study explores the potential of leveraging multiple pre-trained language models, including dialoGPT, BART, T5, and GPT-2, for unsupervised and few-shot analyzing tasks. The results show that a combination of these models, specifically a linearly-weighted combination of dialoGPT and BART, performs well across various tasks, and outperforms a combination of the models in unsupervised and few-shot analyzing. Additionally, the study demonstrates the potential of leveraging few-shot learning to improve the performance of an unsupervised model.

The accuracy of German automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems has been improved by using deep neural networks (DNNs) and data from various applications such as car navigation systems and accessibility tools. Nevertheless, a significant challenge persists due to the limited availability of high-quality public speech datasets. To address this issue, we have developed 'de2', a German ASR platform leveraging hybrid DNN-HMM models, which incorporates several established and unconfirmed speech characteristics. The 'de2' platform also incorporates a range of pre-trained DNN architectures based on common research frameworks like TensorFlow, Theano, and Keras. In order to validate the platform's effectiveness, we have demonstrated how to effectively train and apply a DNN model to phoneme recognition on the 'de2' base dataset 'de2freud+de2m17'. Furthermore, using an accurate phoneme-level translation, we have successfully performed text-to-speech synthesis and achieved a word error rate (WER) of approximately 12% on a commonly used evaluation dataset called the AMI corpus.

The origin of Be-type stars is still unclear with theories involving both single and dual star evolution not having been conclusively ruled out, which requires a thorough analysis of Be-type stars in various environments. To address this knowledge gap, a study focused on Be-type stars within the 30 Doradus region of the Large Magellanic Cloud, a nearby galaxy with a young and rich star cluster, R136. By using spectroscopic data from multiple epochs, we were able to determine the properties of 19 Be-type stars. Our results revealed that 18 stars were intrinsic Be stars, with one being a non-be star during the observation period. We found a binary fraction of 10-20% and detected a possible relationship between the Be-type stars' characteristics and their companion mass. Additionally, we observed minimal variability in the stars' rotation velocity. This study's findings support the presence of a certain type of binary star called a "disk wind" system, further highlighting the need to explore different binary configurations.

To translate ASR output into written text, inverse text normalization is utilized.
Existing ITN techniques, whether data-driven or rule-based, face precise number
pattern challenges. This issue is difficult to resolve via rules and typically
requires data-driven approaches. Nevertheless, data-driven methods are limited
by lack of data, specifically in the context of number patterns which are often
overlooked during collection. To overcome this, we have devised a straightforward
data augmentation technique that generates an abundance of artificial numbers with
distinct formats and are categorized as common number patterns. The resulting
augmented data is then employed to train a sequence-to-sequence model for ITN.
The performance of our model is significantly enhanced by this process, especially
in handling number pattern variations.

This paper demonstrates a Faber-Krahn type inequality for the first eigenvalue 
of the Hermite operator when subject to Robin boundary conditions, showing 
that the optimal configuration is a half-space, and investigates the conditions 
under which equality occurs.

Many procedures in machine learning and genetics are rooted in the concept of learning from related data points, which can be modeled using a graphical model or a Gaussian graphical model. Traditional kernel-based methods often rely on the assumption of exchangeable data, which may not hold in these situations. To address this limitation, we propose a new kernel that accounts for the conditional dependencies between data points, drawing inspiration from the structural tangent space learning framework. Specifically, we derive two non-exchangeable kernel derivatives that are computationally efficient and suitable for large datasets, outperforming standard kernels in various numerical experiments.

Despite numerous studies on non-Hermitian topology, the influence of electron-electron interactions remains unclear. We investigate a one-dimensional non-Hermitian system with significant electron-electron interactions through both the Luttinger liquid theory and many-body Green's function, and find that interaction-induced correlations can reduce the system's topological features by cancelling the non-Hermitian terms. This cancellation leads to an unbroken symmetry and the restoration of the bulk dip in the system's Fermi fluid's momentum distribution, resulting in no fractional excitation spectra in the gapped phases. We further propose that when spin and sub-bands are independently gapped due to non-Hermitian terms, but exhibit equal gaps when the terms are negligible, the correlations will restore the topological features, separating scenarios where topological features can and cannot be restored. Our findings also suggest that correlations and gapped phases mutually enhance each other's stabilities, and propose an explanation for the recent observations of seemingly 'unphysical' topological features in pseudo-spin and charge degrees of freedom separately. We also identify our system as an example of spontaneous pseudo-Hermitian symmetry breaking. We further propose several experiments that can directly observe the topological features and phase transitions in one-dimensional non-Hermitian systems, including quantum Monte Carlo sampling, interference in CNP, generative modeling, and electron energy loss spectroscopy.

Our research focuses on developing a communication system that is more natural and engaging for listeners. We've made significant breakthroughs in creating social attributes in synthetic speech, including a perceived femininity and youthfulness, which are essential for building connections between people and machines. Our previous studies showed that these social attributes affect how people interact with their devices. We've now explored new ways to incorporate social traits into synthetic speech, specifically by adjusting the speaker's confidence and friendliness levels. Using a cutting-edge text-to-speech system, we've successfully incorporated these social attributes and presented a study to the IEEE Workshop on Electronic Commerce, where we discussed the possibilities of incorporating these features to make interactions between humans and machines more enjoyable and personalized.

A radiative seesaw model incorporating light dark matter and featuring modular A4 and gauged U(1)_(B-L) symmetries is proposed, where neutrino masses are produced through one-loop interactions, resulting in a dark matter mass of keV. Modularity introduces new constraints, particularly on the dark matter mass, that arise from mixing between Kaluza-Kaleno states and modular reparameterization. Additionally, the model's predictions for neutrino masses and mixings are restricted by light dark matter density and neutrinoless double beta decay criteria. Specifically, the model's lightest neutrino mass can be as large as 0.8 mEe and several order magnitudes larger than the experimental upper bound is explored.

In triaxial nuclei, the intrinsic axis of an angular momentum vector deviates from the equilibrium state due to their inherent octupole shape. In this study, the Gogny Hamiltonian's corresponding mean field dynamics for low-lying quasi-proton $3\pi$ $0^+$ states in even-even isotopes is investigated using the wavelet expansion formalism with a specific range for the intrinsic angular momentum vector, taking into account a minimum length for the space. The calculations, performed for a range of isotopes around the octupole phenomenon area, show that a specific length value can restore the dynamics that was lost in the standard mean field dynamics along with an intrinsic axis deviation, known as the orientation, that naturally arises from the wave function without additional constraints. The study also finds that triaxiality plays a significant role in describing octupole states in nuclei and that a specific length value, which varies with mass number, is required to restore intrinsic axis deviations that naturally arise in this system.

This paper proposes 4-phase, 6-phase, 8-phase, and 16-phase, 24-phase, 26-phase
and 28-phase Golay complementary array designs, along with their respective frequency
algebra constructions and occurrences. These arrays will likely be applied in the areas
of array signal processing and Golay complementary sequences, respectively.

Incorporating the benefits of both deep learning methods and neuromodulator architectures, this research proposes an unsupervised change detection approach for multi-image series, specifically tailored for hyperspectral images. By adapting a deep convolutional neuromodulator model to accommodate three-dimensional spectral data, the framework enables detection of alterations within images across multiple spectral dimensions. Furthermore, a novel extension of the Saliency-based Deep Neuromodulator is introduced, leveraging salient feature extraction to enhance the detection of significant changes. To improve performance, a modified version of the extension is trained in an unsupervised manner using a self-supervised approach. To validate the effectiveness of the proposed methods, comprehensive experimental analysis is conducted on multiple datasets, demonstrating their superior performance compared to alternative state-of-the-art approaches.

Gromeka and Stillinger introduced residual entropy as a way to examine cavity formation in molecular liquids, discovering a link between entropy and viscosity. Following their discovery, researchers for the first time theoretically quantified the relative entropy and viscosity of molecular liquids. In a series of Monte Carlo simulations, we explored this connection in detail for seven distinct molecular liquids by comparing relative entropy and viscosity generated by parallelized simulations, all based on pairwise potentials, for various coupling strengths and temperatures. Additionally, we conducted pair distribution function analyses and determined the optimal coupling strength for each liquid that balances accuracy in entropy and viscosity.
