Recent advancements in quantum simulation using quantum computing have yielded significant insights into the behavior of complex many-body systems, particularly those governed by non-linear Hamiltonians, through the application of analog quantum simulators, as well as digital simulators. Nonetheless, efficiently modeling systems with an equal number of up-spin and down-spin particles that interact via the Hubbard interaction - particularly those in the anti-ferromagnetic phase - has proven challenging using digital quantum computing methods due to its inherent risk of causing a wave function collapse onto a trivial configuration with no spin. To address this issue, our approach proposes a hybrid digital-analog simulation technique that utilizes an analog quantum computer to represent the fermions' spin states and digital control to manage the connections between them, thereby mitigating wave function collapse and efficiently simulating interactions. Through this method, our experiments show that anti-ferromagnetic phase emergence can be efficiently replicated when 4 particles are present, while the phenomenon is lost when more particles are added due to the wave function collapsing onto a trivial configuration. Our research also showcases a new way to simulate complex many-body systems, particularly those in the anti-fermagnetic phase, using a hybrid digital-analog technique that leverages analog quantum computers to represent the interactions between particles.

Graph polynomials hold significant value due to their potential to derive numerical characteristics of graphs, which can be applied to various complex problems. Certain problems feature recursive structures, and in some cases, overcoming recursive obstacles is crucial for understanding the degree of polynomial's growth. Researchers often explore the degree of polynomials, and in doing so, often focus on a single graph. However, by combining multiple graphs, new and intriguing results can be achieved. A recently discovered set of graph polynomials, known as multi-graph polynomials, was found to be connected to the properties of a particular set of differential equations. Through multi-graph polynomials, and specifically a particular combination, we achieve a solution to a long-standing problem concerning the complexity of the graph isomorphism problem, and we also find that this problem is further linked to another concept known as the graph monic sum of powers. Furthermore, we achieve a single unified explanation for several known results concerning the rate of polynomial growth, and we also find that this rate of growth for multi-graph polynomials is influenced by certain properties of the underlying graphs. We achieve a comprehensive understanding of the degree of polynomial growth through multi-graph polynomials, and we also find that this particular combination is associated with a concept known as graph flow.

We find an optimal transformation, known as a hitchin configuration, for a specific type of curve that follows a mathematical formula. This curve, which is called the Veech curve, is made up of a combination of polynomials with various degrees and is also a member of a special class of curves that have a limited number of points of intersection when two or more polynomials meet. Our solution involves a complex mathematical proof that relies on the intersection of these polynomials changing in a specific way as one variable changes. Along with this, we discovered a new collection of simple plane curves that can be used to prove that the points of intersection of these curves, which are all part of this hitchin configuration, have a common characteristic when counted, known as a mathematical divisor. This collection of curves can also be used to prove that the points of intersection of these curves, which are all part of this hitchin configuration, are connected in a specific way to a particular mathematical concept, known as a fundamental region. Additionally, one of these simple plane curves, which is also a member of this hitchin configuration, is particularly notable because it has a specific mathematical property called a Wieferich number. This number, which is also a number that can be repeated," is particularly notable because it has a specific mathematical property called a Wilson prime. This number, which is also a number that can be repeated," is particularly notable because it has a specific mathematical property called a palindrome.

The shift to working from home, triggered by the COVID-19 pandemic, has led to an accelerated transformation, where more people than ever are adopting remote work and project management approaches such as Scrum. Despite home work's widespread adoption, there's still considerable uncertainty about its impact on Scrum projects. This study aims to explore this question by a multi-method design that incorporates quantitative data analysis, qualitative content analysis of existing research, and surveys targeting professionals working from home in general, and Scrum masters and developers in particular. By examining the influence of remote work on Scrum projects, this research aims to identify the key factors that could explain variations in project success outcomes and provide practical recommendations for Scrum projects to optimize their performance when implemented remotely.

The article further explores certain concepts related to the set of non-singular arrowhead matrices, which was previously established over the field of two complex numbers in 2019 by Wu and Gau, to derive the normalized permanent and determinant of specific 4x4 non-singular arrowhead matrices. Additionally, it introduces a new set of more general arrowhead matrices over the field of n complex numbers and investigates the relationship between their generalized column and row arrowhead matrices. Furthermore, it presents several duplication and partition methods for these general matrices. By applying these general matrices, it calculates the normalized permanent and determinant of specific 4x4 non-singular arrowhead matrices in terms of generalized integer Bell numbers and their rational forms. Lastly, it discusses certain potential applications and extensions of these general matrices.

In a study using the ALICE detector at the LHC, scientists investigated the elliptical movement of electrons resulting from the decay of charm particles after Pb-Pb collisions at a high energy of 5.02 TeV. These electrons, called inclusive J/$\psi$-tagged electrons, were examined based on nearly 22 nanobarns of data collected in 2015 and 2016. Research revealed a noticeable difference in their movement during non-central collisions, assigning a temperature of around 274 ± 16 ± 4 unknown variables. These findings are in line with predictions from relativistic heavy-ion collisions models, supporting the formation of a quark-gluon plasma state in such collisions. Additionally, scientists found a relationship between the elliptical movement of these electrons and collision energy, with observed patterns consistent across different collision energies. These results provide a key test of the formation of quark-gluon plasma in such collisions, with observed agreements offering further support for this phenomenon.

In pursuit of breakthroughs in machine learning, the concept of algebraic topology has been incorporated into AI research over recent years. This work represents a progression in the topological design of generative neural networks, focusing on the development of novel methods to generate institutional corpora through learning and prediction tasks. A central role is assigned to the chromatic alpha structure, which embodies the inherent characteristics of classification problems. By utilizing the homogeneous expansion of chromatic alpha structures via the distributive law with free monoids, the persistent homology of these topological structures can be analyzed. It has been established that the persistent homology of chromatic alpha structures holds significant predictive value. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that the incorporation of additional corpora leads to enhancements in the predictive capabilities of these topological structures.

The extremal group delay distortion (GDoF) performance differences between optimal and binary power control (BPC) have been investigated in a network with multiple ($K$) users where all users receive and transmit simultaneously. In this network, when every user uses BPC, each user's transmission is assigned a fixed percentage of the available spectrum. As the number of users ($K$) doubles, the GDoF performance is shown to degrade from 1 to approximately $\frac{1}{\sqrt{K}}$ in the limit. In contrast, when each user employs optimal power control, their respective transmission bandwidths vary based on their individual characteristics, leading to improved GDoF performance in this network. Auditing is receiving increasing attention as a result of the growing need to incorporate human knowledge and understanding into the process. One of the key decisions an auditor must make is categorization, whether it's regarding a company's risk or the detection of fraudulent behavior. These categorizations are typically subjective and can vary greatly between different levels of expertise. This research proposes a new method of categorization that's both adaptable and explicit. It allows for an expert's experience to influence their decision, with more experienced individuals creating more refined concepts. Employing Formal Concept Analysis (FCA) and the Dempster-Shafer (DS) theory, this study defines and evaluates several categorization approaches. These approaches are tested in two real-world scenarios: auditing a company's risk and the detection of cyber-attacks. The approach utilizing DS theory is found to outperform less complex methods, providing more accurate results.

The creation of artificial island landscapes holds significant importance in numerous fields such as geography, ecology, computer science, economics, and urban planning due to its versatility. Applications include generating mock island geologies for scientific research and constructing personalized, engaging virtual environments in video games. A key challenge in island creation is achieving a balance between artistic control and environmental factors such as coastline, altitude, and vegetation. In this research paper, we address this challenge by controlling island features through a combination of existing examples and a stitching technique based on level set method to facilitate explicit surface manipulation. Our innovative generation method allows for precise control over interconnecting individual islands while adjusting coastline, altitude, and other surface features. Our approach can also simulate natural processes and predict island states over time. In this study, we showcase the potential of our technique by showcasing the results of manual island creations and automated simulations.

In the context of the generalized uncertainty principle, modifications to the Lorentz and Galilean transformations emerge in the form of asymptotic equations, with velocities exceeding the uncertainty principle threshold velocity $v_{u}$ giving rise to distinct outcomes. The Lorentz transformation reveals a shift from special to relativistic kinetics at a substantial threshold of $v_{u} \approx 3.51$. The analysis shows that a gravitational potential influences the Lorentz transformation, causing a mix of kinetic and potential energy in the Lorentz relation via a small potential shift proportional to $(v_{u}/c) ^2$. The investigation of the GUP impact also explores a range of phenomena from GUP to Lorentz violation, discussing its relevance to cosmological observations and laboratory experiments, as well as assessing various formulations of GUP.

We consider a problem in which we have a set of periods, each with corresponding demand quantities and a limit on available processing capabilities. Our objective is to determine the duration of partial processing capabilities for each period, which would optimize the total number of periods processed across all time periods and processing levels. To address this issue, we first develop a polynomial-time solution for a straightforward processing allocation problem with modular requirements. Our results for this base case enable us to derive a general, approximately-optimal algorithm for the more complex demand quantities problem, which provides a performance guarantee of $4$ and can be tightened to $3+1/k$ (and ultimately, for infinite $k$, to $\frac{4}{3}$).

This research investigates a single-legged hopping robot moving on a deformable surface. To enhance its mobility, the robot is equipped with a pseudo-liquid appendage that attaches to its ankle, which allows it to manipulate the terrain's stiffness and adapt to changing terrain types. Through computational modeling, the researchers examined a hopping robot moving on a half-sine surface covered in a nonlinear liquid-like material. To simplify this complex system, it was divided into two separate regions: the single-legged hopping robot and the liquid-like material. Both components are interconnected through established relationships that define their interdependent dynamics. To resolve the resulting system of equations, the researchers used the Euler method paired with a series of iterative Newton-Raphson calculations. This computational method successfully modeled the robot's motion and allowed the researchers to examine how the liquid-like material influences its hopping pattern. To assess the liquid-like material's effectiveness, the researchers evaluated the robot's stability and found that certain texture variations could significantly enhance its stability by adjusting specific parameters such as phase lag, phase coefficient, and liquid-like material stiffness, particularly when certain parameters were optimized in conjunction with one another.

In the rapidly evolving landscape of Internet of Things (IoT) networks, periodic firmware updates are crucial for maintaining security and reliability. Given the trend towards implementing security measures via code-based updates, and the existing literature on large-scale firmware updates, we concentrate on the mesh network paradigm. This study assesses two leading mesh protocols, 802.11s and Zigbee, by evaluating a substantial mesh network comprising 100 nodes and scrutinizing the impact of mesh size, signal strength variation, wireless interference, and firmware size on dependability in both protocols. Furthermore, we introduce an innovative method for generating and evaluating fault trees to analyze system reliability. Our comprehensive evaluation provides thorough insight into the practical implications of rolling out firmware updates across vast IoT networks.

We examine a one-dimensional system of multiple particles with attractive interaction, coupled to a heat bath that represents its surroundings. Our focus is on how this system behaves as it undergoes a phase shift from a non-thermal state to a thermal equilibrium. By using a mathematical representation of the system's wave functions, we are able to identify key characteristics related to its thermal behavior. These include the rate at which this system's energy distribution evolves and the complexity of its energy levels. Our findings indicate a specific pattern in this complexity that characterizes non-thermal behavior. Additionally, we observe a significant discrepancy between the system's expected thermal behavior and actual behavior near the point at which the phase shift occurs. This discrepancy is a sign of a significant within-phase shift in the system's thermal characteristics.

This paper addresses a novel problem of finding multiple hidden objects behind a hidden barrier by asking a single agent for information through a single channel, with each request providing only "yes" or "no" answers that don't give away their location of origin. Although this scenario was first explored in a non-interactive setting by Kleiman et al. at ICALP 2019, this research focuses on the more complex multi-target variant. By combining recent findings from Kleiman et al., we gain two key insights: a lower bound and an exact solution that uses an adaptive version of their original query for searching a single target. Interestingly, using this exact solution yields nearly optimal results when searching for a single target, and surprisingly, it also provides a reasonably good performance for the multi-target problem. Moreover, we also show that by using a specific non-adaptive query, it is possible to achieve a performance that is relatively close to the multi-target variant of the original query. Overall, we find that these existing solutions, although not optimal themselves, can be leveraged to provide valuable insights and guide the search for better, more optimal solutions in this complex problem.

The exploration of universal perturbations and adversarial instances within the context of quantum classifiers is still an underdeveloped area of research. It has been established that quantum classifiers can be susceptible to universal adversarial instances that induce incorrect classifications regardless of the input state |x>. These instances, in turn, have been shown to originate from minimal distortions of the input data. In an attempt to address the scarcity of research, we have conducted thorough examinations of the phenomenon. Our study begins by applying a quantum abstraction of the concept to introduce a universal perturbation scheme for quantum classifiers. This scheme, which can be viewed as a quantum variation of the well-known adversarial saliency map method, highlights the significance of input features in determining the classifier's output. By developing a universal perturbation scheme for quantum classifiers, we have demonstrated its potential to uncover hidden patterns within the data through the application of a genetic algorithm. In addition, we have demonstrated that this scheme converges asymptotically towards the natural gradient of the data. In an effort to understand the underlying causes of the phenomenon, we have explored the relationship between the rank of the natural gradient and its norm, establishing upper and lower bounds for specific types of data. Lastly, we have illustrated the efficacy of the universal perturbation scheme through its application in data compression.

Our study concerns Steklov eigenvalues in nearly round 2D domains, where we initially identify lower and upper bounds for these eigenvalues in nearly round domains of fixed area, and then convert these bounds into a logarithmic estimate. Subsequently, we present a theorem that addresses the rate at which Steklov eigenvalues change in response to perturbations in a nearly round domain, where we also take into account the dependence on the perturbation. Notably, this result has implications for us to asymptotically determine the Steklov eigenvalues for domains that are topologically equivalent to the unit disk.

In applications where data is exchanged between businesses, processes are defined according to a set of rules and specifications, known as a process definition, within a framework known as a process notation such as XPDL or CP-narratives. Implementations of these processes are then evaluated based on how well they adhere to these predefined rules and specifications, which can be achieved through the use of a formal tool that checks for conformity.

A particular approach to checking for conformity in applications involves comparing actual process traces to expected process traces, which can be represented using a process definition. Past methods for achieving this comparison, such as through prefix alignments, have demonstrated certain limitations in handling situations where the expected and actual process traces have differing lengths or if multiple instances of a given element occur in the expected process trace.

In an effort to address these limitations, a novel method for checking for conformity has been developed and demonstrated using real-world examples, which aligns portions of the expected and actual process traces based on the order in which they occur, their lengths, and the elements contained within them. Additionally, this approach can be refined by incorporating semantic relationships between the elements of the process definition, which can provide a more nuanced evaluation of adherence to the expected process traces.

Radio signal prediction has become a crucial task due to the growing reliance on wireless networks. Accurate prediction of radio signal strength is essential to determine coverage and plan networks effectively, particularly in new areas where coverage data may not be available. While computational models such as ray launching can predict signals with high accuracy, they are resource-intensive and not suitable for rapid coverage planning in new areas due to their computational intensity. An alternative widely used method for predicting radio signals is empirical modeling, which uses statistical data on signal attenuation due to certain factors. However, this type of model has limitations in its applicability and can't account for unknown factors during deployment. A recent approach to address this need is a data-driven method called Radio Map Generation, which uses machine learning to generate models that can predict radio signals with high accuracy. An enhanced version of this method, called Deep RMG, is proposed in this research, which uses a more sophisticated approach to capture complex signal interactions while maintaining scalability for large networks. The proposed method is compared against other latest approaches and shows significant performance improvements, validating its potential as a powerful tool for rapid coverage planning in new areas.

A straightforward semantics is proposed for temporal planning. We define and formally establish the logic within the interactive theorem prover Isabelle/HOL, and then establish a formal proof of forward inference, utilizing these established foundations to build a verification tool for checking temporal planning programs. We apply this tool to validate the correctness of existing air traffic control planning algorithms.

Power system expansion planning models are being used increasingly to incorporate external costs of power generation. These external costs represent factors such as air pollution and renewable energy policy requirements. However, the key challenges lie in accurately translating the external costs into technology-specific prices and addressing the responsiveness of the model. This study used a multi-period model of the power system spanning from 2020 to2035, factoring in generation costs, transmission constraints, demand response, and external costs related to renewable energy technology-specific carbon emissions. The model's key variables include line flows, power prices, and generation levels. The model's responsiveness was assessed by adjusting selected variables and re-running the model in both open and closed-loop scenarios. The results showed that the model significantly reacts to generation capacity in terms of power prices, with a one-megawatt increase in capacity resulting in a price reduction of around 4-5 dollars per megawatt-hour. The study found that the model's response to other variables is significant, indicating a high degree of uncertainty in modeling results. Additionally, the results highlight the model's preference for incorporating flexible generation capacity with the least increment in investment costs.

This study establishes the global existence of classical solutions for the Vlasov-Poisson and the ionic Vlasov-Poisson models within confined areas, under specified boundary conditions that include a particular reflection scenario for the Vlasov equation.

When performing maintenance on software projects, developers often receive multiple, loosely related requests for change, described using varying vocabulary and style. Assessing and respond to these changes efficiently requires Concept Location, a task that poses difficulties due to the unstructured and unorganized nature of software code and related change requests. Previous studies and tools failed to fully address this issue, leaving a significant gap in research. This paper presents a new approach, STRICT, which leverages predictive modeling and IR techniques to rapidly pinpoint change request concepts in software code. We extracted two datasets from the Maintenance Track of the TREC suite and utilized them to train a search tool using the Rapid Automatic Reconfiguration framework. We compared our approach with existing tools, assessing their performance using precision, recall, F1-measure, and processing time metrics. Results demonstrate that STRICT significantly outperforms other methods, showing improved accuracy and efficiency by 49% and 0.9 seconds respectively.

Researchers have discovered a new technique to improve the mobility of colloidal gels by using ultrasonic vibrations. When subjected to these high-frequency sound waves, the gels undergo structural changes at the particle level, becoming more rigid and rigidified states are formed.  The influence of ultrasonic vibrations on the gels' mechanical properties, such as their yield stress and strain, varies based on gel concentration and vibration intensity. A lower gel concentration benefits from ultrasonic treatment, as it leads to gels with lower yield stress but higher strain. However, a higher concentration of gels results in ultrasonic vibration resistance, making it harder to apply. Despite these challenges, ultrasonic treatment of concentrated gels yields gels with low yield stress but high flowability. The effect of ultrasonic treatment on the gels' flow characteristics is most noticeable when vibrations are intense, leading to improved flowability. The flow improvements in the gels are largely due to ultrasonic treatment disruptions at the gel's structural network. The gels' flow improvements also reduce the friction between particles. The discovery of rheological effects of ultrasonic treatment opens new avenues in gel colloid science and the possible applications in transport of solids through fluids.

The Collatz Conjecture is a well-known phenomenon in number theory that has remained unproven for nearly a century yet continues to captivate mathematicians. It's easy to understand its foundation: as a starting point, any given number is either entirely divinely divided by 2, or it's odd and can only be transformed by multiplying it by 3 and adding 1. Its essence lies in its algorithm, or the sequence of number transformations it entails. Several renowned mathematicians, including Alan Turing, have attempted to validate this algorithm, although it remains unverified to this day. Yet, in the past few years, the majority of comprehensive checks have yielded supportive results, strengthening the Collatz Conjecture's likelihood of being true. Nonetheless, the fact that no one has found a clear pattern or underlying proof indicates that it still holds significant unresolved complexity. This paper aims to simplify our comprehension of the Collatz by analyzing its underlying characteristics and testing various patterns, or else confirming its universal applicability through the creation of a new classification system that categorizes numbers into distinct groups based on their behavior in the sequence, or the sequence of number transformations it entails.

In the realm of STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics) communication, understanding the category to which a document belongs is crucial. Essentially, category-inference is a form of multi-label classification. Historically, mathematical notations have posed difficulties for information extraction systems, which have consistently been treated as distinct entities rather than integrated into the surrounding English text. This separation can cause problems in extracting meaningful information, particularly when it comes to the context required for multi-label classification in STEM documents. To address this, we've developed a unique approach for STEM document category classification by integrating mathematical notation context through a technique called ME-LINK, which identifies entity links specific to mathematics. By experimenting with the combination of ME-LINK and a neural language model that preserves the interdependence of words in the document, our results have shown a notable improvement in multi-label classification accuracy.

This study focuses on creating a more efficient approach to the stable marriage problem over time. Within this framework, participants in the market arrive over time and must decide whether to propose marriages or not. Previous research explored strategies for potential suitors to employ when deciding whether to initiate or refrain from a particular marriage, resulting in the creation of a theoretical framework called "strategy sketches." Building upon this previous work, we aim to explore and compare different "sketchs" that can lead to the establishment of long-term, stable relationships over time. Through application of a theoretical concept called "approximate welfare loss," we define and identify a particular sketch that is considered the most effective at achieving long-term stability and demonstrate how this sketch's performance can be impacted by the timing and frequency of new arrivals in the market. Moreover, our analysis demonstrates how the complexity of this problem can be broken down into more manageable parts using probabilistic concepts. Ultimately, we support our findings with numerical data that highlights the trade-off between the risk of temporary unsatisfying matches and the likelihood of achieving long-term stability and its relationship with the arrival rate in the market.

Current evaluation metrics for summarization models are inadequate, as they are
highly model-dependent and fail to align with human judgments of summary quality.
To resolve this, we introduce SummScore, the first comprehensive assessment metric
that scores the overall quality of summaries by considering both coherence and
accuracy in terms of content. We propose a Cross-Encoder architecture to generate
scores that outperform existing metrics and demonstrate greater alignment with
human judgments. Additionally, SummScore is accompanied by a robust ScoreAnnot
tool, designed to facilitate metric training with high-quality annotations.
Both SummScore and the ScoreAnnot tool are openly available for use at
https://github.com/techsing/SummScore.

Compressive sensing theory shows that sparse signals can be accurately recovered from a limited number of measurements. This research presents a new method of measurement that not only provides better resistance to noise but also enables the recovery of signals in an extremely shorter amount of time. This new method is based on a quadratic formulation and takes advantage of the unique properties of signals with lower degrees of nonlinearity. As a result, it significantly outperforms traditional methods in both robustness and runtime for signals with these characteristics, while remaining competitive for signals with more complex nonlinearity.

The combination of LiDAR and camera data is crucial for many autonomous vehicles and robotic systems using LiDAR. We propose the BEVFusion framework, a straightforward and efficient method for fusing LiDAR and camera data in a beacon-based level, which outperforms existing fusion techniques. The key to our approach is a lightweight flow extractor that adapts a camera image to a LiDAR beamline, and a flow integrator that matches extracted flows with nearby LiDAR beams. The extracted flows are then ranked based on their quality and priority. To further enhance our method's accuracy, we propose two quality assessment modules, incorporating a feature learning mechanism and a classification network, respectively, to evaluate the quality of each flow. Our approach has been successfully tested on the NANO dataset and the KITTI dataset, demonstrating significantly improved performance in detecting objects and tracking their movement. The code and models underlying our approach are available on the GitHub repository at https://github.com/CCF-USTC/BEVFusion.

In the context of magnetohydrodynamics, a thermal disturbance is considered, assumed to be non-intermittent and self-similar in the "inertial range" that lies between the sources and the dissipation range. In this region, it's shown that the thermal disturbance "amplitude" follows a specific scaling variation, which bears a resemblance to the scaling observed in vortices. Furthermore, this variation is associated "with the time it takes for energy to be transferred" from one scale to a smaller one, specifically a scale of the order of the collision rate. In the dissipation range, which is characterized by a Kolmogorov scale, the thermal disturbance "amplitude" increases without bound as it approaches this limit, diverging in a specific manner in relation to the collision rate. This specific relation enables an understanding of how the thermal disturbance "amplitude" behaves in the collisionless regime, which in turn yields a specific scaling of the thermal disturbance "amplitude" in terms of the collision rate. It is proposed that this specific scaling variation is applicable not only to MHD but also to Navier-Stokes fluid turbulence. Moreover, it's argued that any non-MHD thermal disturbance in the far-infrared to microwave band can be modeled using the above fluid turbulence model, which in turn enables an understanding of the relationship between the collision rate and temperature differences, thereby allowing for the calculation of such differences.

The self-focusing effect in a highly nonlinear medium, such as water, leads to intricate light patterns and diffractive loss. Although the process is well understood, precise control of self-focusing is hindered by unpredictability. To shed light on the matter, researchers have closely examined the thermal effects produced by the laser in the medium. They employed an advanced simulation method, incorporating non-rigid-body dynamics to model the medium's response and resulting heat patterns. The model reveals that heat patterns differ significantly from those predicted by simple models, contributing to complex self-induced diffraction patterns. The developed model serves as a comprehensive reference for insight into the non-rigid medium's interaction with light, ultimately enabling the design of controlled self-phase matching techniques.

When using neural models to analyze design discussions extracted from documents, a change in the document often results in different design elements being extracted. However, the consistency of the design extraction when the document remains the same should be significantly higher than when the document changes. We developed new methods to conclude about a design's elements based on documents by using natural language. These methods involve both simulated data analysis and real-world design discussions, aiming to identify a design's key aspects. Through testing, it becomes evident that training classifiers on both design and discuss datasets leads to better performance compared to training only on design datasets. Additionally, incorporating discuss datasets leads to a more precise understanding of the design's elements.

This paper presents a solution for processing continuous queries in streaming data, incorporating both temporal and spatial components. We propose a novel runtime architecture, consisting of a distributed'stream processor', for each service required in the query, that leverages microservices design. Each service utilizes a shared memory cache, enabling rapid data retrieval from distributed data storage, and facilitating efficient processing of both streaming and historical data. We validate the effectiveness and performance of our approach through experiments on multiple microservices and demo trials showcasing real-world applications.

In scenarios involving single particles beyond the Standard Model, specifically top and bottom companions, $t_5$ and $b_5$, the observations at the Large Hadron Collider seem to indicate that their production is less frequent than expected. To resolve this discrepancy, the focus lies on the non-resonant contributions from effective, higher-dimensional operators that influence the interactions between these particles and standard model fermions. It has been discovered that, at the two-loop level, the non-resonant corrections to top and bottom partner production are substantially higher than expected and could significantly impact various phenomenological studies, leading to the conclusion that resonant and non-resonant contributions must be examined simultaneously within the same theoretical framework to accurately analyze single partner production at the Large Hadron Collider.

A recent breakthrough in translating English to SPARQL via neural machine translation (NMT) shows great potential, but dealing with structured knowledge base data within SPARQL queries remains a significant challenge. To address this, the proposed copy system incorporates copying mechanisms from established machine translation frameworks to enable SPARQL NMT to extract and replicate individual knowledge base elements, especially useful when part of a larger triple, from the input query. Leveraging these copying mechanisms leads to an improved translation quality and robustness in handling varied input data. Moreover, due to reduced reliance on pre-built knowledge base vocabularies, the proposed approach enhances the versatility of SPARQL NMT. Experiments using both real and artificially generated data sets demonstrate that the proposed copy system delivers a notable improvement in translation accuracy, specifically by at least 14.2% and 11.6% in terms of recall and precision, respectively, and an overall substantial gain in formal accuracy, exceeding 85.9% and outperforms the baseline model in various established evaluation metrics. Furthermore, the proposed system offers a substantial improvement in handling input queries with irreducible subjects, and an assessment of its translation by humans confirms that it meets their expectations. Notably, the proposed approach outperforms its closest competitor, SP2RL, and significantly outperforms a recently proposed SPARQL NMT model, and it is expected that this approach will help drive future research in this field.

This work reveals the significance of publication venues in evaluating researchers and institutions. By examining a comprehensive dataset of over 1.5 million scholarly articles, our study provides new insights on the impact of venues on the impact of individual researchers and institutions, and verifies the limitations of using citation metrics to measure their performance. To overcome these limitations, our analysis introduces a set of comprehensive venue metrics that can accurately capture the research productivity of various venues and indirectly evaluate the productivity of their authors and institutions. These innovative metrics can be easily computed from a comprehensive scholarly dataset, and our analysis demonstrates their substantial differences in values, highlighting their potential to provide a more accurate representation of research productivity in practice. Furthermore, by classifying and grouping venues based on these metrics, we can gain a clearer understanding of which authors and institutions are thriving in particular fields and disciplines. Overall, our study offers a set of simple yet effective metrics for accurately evaluating the research productivity of various venues, which can help to develop new indicators to identify top performers in academia. These indicators can be easily computed from large scholarly datasets, and are particularly useful when citation data is limited or unreliable. Additionally, our analysis enables the systematic classification and grouping of scholarly venues based on their research productivity. These findings have significant implications for academia, where understanding and recognizing top performers is crucial for recognizing achievements and influencing research priorities. Finally, our analysis highlights the significance of publication venues as a means to influence research priorities, influence the selection of publication channels, and recognize top performers in academia.

The growing presence of black-box artificial intelligence models in control systems poses challenges in ensuring their reliability, particularly with regards to their effective operation within their expected range of parameters and their capacity to adapt to unforeseen circumstances. Researchers in the control field are actively investigating methods to address these concerns through analysis and modeling of the neural networks' behavior. This work provides an overview of the current developments in analyzing the behavior of the neural networks, particularly with regards to their robustness and adaptability.

This study introduces novel functorial frameworks for statistical quantities that capture data set characteristics across varying scales. In computational biology, hierarchical clustering is used to categorize data such as genes, proteins, or Dependent variable expressions, based on their intrinsic properties. However, traditional methods often overlook crucial aspects as they combine nearby elements, forgetting hierarchical relationships. To rectify this, region-functor based clustering is developed, incorporating hierarchical groupings with overlapping regions. Furthermore, domain-specific mean and median functors are proposed, allowing for robustness in handling outliers. Empirical comparisons showcase the superiority of our approach on real-world expression data. Lastly, the proposed method is demonstrated through its application in analyzing chromatin compaction using Hi-C technology.

The demand for efficient visual data recovery methods is increasing rapidly due to advancements in streaming media. Existing techniques, such as neural data completion, struggle when applied to 3D tensor data retrieved through internet streaming. To address this challenge, this research introduces the Patch Tracking-based Streaming Tensor Loop Completion (PSTL-C) method, designed to complete missing values in 3D tensors being transmitted over the internet. By leveraging the concepts of data tracking and completion, this innovative approach tackles the problem of recovering streaming tensor loops (SRLs) in a real-time streaming environment. Building on the principles of dynamic association and completion, it uses patch tracking to efficiently complete missing values in each tensor loop, based on previous and upcoming patches from incoming tensors. To demonstrate its practicality, this method is implemented using a streaming video playback system, which simulates real-time tensor streaming and data recovery. Experimental evaluations of PSTL-C demonstrate its superiority over existing completion techniques on various datasets, across multiple evaluation metrics and scenarios.

It is demonstrated that in cases where the Lie types of groups associated with Weyl groups fall under A, B, C, or D, their Nichols algebras exhibit the property of being infinite-dimensional. Moreover, a formula for calculating the infinite-dimensional Nichols algebras directly, based on specific parameters associated with these groups, has been established and used in numerous examples.

One of the primary goals in understanding wave turbulence is to develop a physically accurate mathematical model that can describe long-term time evolution of a system composed of weakly nonlinear waves in the presence of weak energy dissipation. Researchers have shown that in the wave energy range with a frequency lower than the dissipation frequency, this model leads to a closed loop equation, known as the Zakharov equation, which yields the Khairullin-Osorio-Kulichkin equation after introducing an average energy density, with the resulting solution exhibiting infinite energy flux and an frequency spectrum following the $f^{-5/3}$ pattern. However, in this study, the solution's accuracy is assessed through comparison with high-resolution numerical simulations of the fully nonlinear wave equation. Interestingly, the in-vacuo Khairullin-Osorio-Kulichkin equation's solution fails to represent the actual turbulent wave spectrum, which is instead found to align with the $f^{-5/3}$ pattern only after accounting for the effects of dissipation.

We examine a family of methods derived from iteratively applying a graph normalization step, coupled with random node selection and deletion, followed by node addition, starting with an initial input graph $G$. This technique is motivated by a desire to create a sparse, structured graph suitable for subsequent processing. We aim to understand the output graph properties after terminating this procedure at a specified time $t$ with the maximum-weight fully independent subgraph, denoted as $\mathcal{M}_t(G)$. While it is clear that each iteration tends to increase the size of the largest independent set, the behavior becomes more complex when considering the influence on the largest matching set size. We explore the limitations in controlling the overfitting tendency of over-growth of the largest matching set during the normalization process. Despite this complexity, we propose an algorithm that efficiently determines the optimal time $t^*$ to terminate the normalization procedure in order to achieve the largest and most sparse fully independent subgraph. This method works by analyzing the growth rates of the largest matching and independent set sizes over iterations. Notably, our method has a $O(E\log V)$ time complexity, where $E$ represents the number of edges and $V$ represents the number of vertices in the graph $G$. We validate the effectiveness of our method by providing empirical evidence from various real-world applications involving data such as link prediction, node screening, and the detection of densely clustered communities.

This research studies the electronic transport characteristics of a graphene field-effect transistor (FET) to explore its behavior under external stimuli that vary with time. By controlling the FET with a modulated gate potential, the constraints imposed by the device's package on charge transport can be examined. Our analysis shows that the current induced by a given modulation is directly linked to the time-dependent conductivity of the device and the effect of its capacitance connections. Our findings indicate that as temperature increases, so too does the conductivity of the device, ultimately leading to a significant increase in its current output. Conversely, at low temperatures, the current is largely diminished. Furthermore, our analysis shows that the energy dissipated by the device is influenced by its temperature and the external modulation frequency. For instance, at higher frequencies, the energy dissipation is largely confined to a particular energy range, whereas at lower frequencies, the energy dissipation spreads across a broader range. By utilizing the multiple plateaux phenomenon in the device's conductance, we are able to precisely determine its effective temperature. Our analysis also shows that using a finite modulation frequency instead of a step function can reduce this effective temperature, whereas using an finite duration gate signal can actually increase it. Lastly, our model illustrates how the thermal characteristics of the device are affected by its finite size, and our analytical findings demonstrate that the current output, power, and energy dissipation all exhibit proportional relationships with the external modulation frequency.

The 2I/r radio continuum emission from CR Dra in active binary systems is an exceptional example of the electron-cyclotron maser (ECM) mechanism, exhibiting extremely long and consistent periods.  First discovered in 1985, CR Dra's 2I/r radiation, in the form of a steady, mHz low-frequency emission, presented a challenge to the ECM theory due to its persistent nature.  The ECM is typically associated with magnetic flux tubes in inactive binary systems, decaying over years in typical cases.  Our long-term, detailed, low-frequency observations from the Murchison Widefield Array began in 2018 and have continued through 2021, providing an in-depth analysis of CR Dra's radio emission.  We have also conducted simultaneous optical observations to establish the system's activity level.  Our findings, covering a time-frame from 2018 March to 2019 February and 2019 November to 2019 December, showed a unique radio burst in late-2019 as well as a persistent, level of 2I/r radiation in the mHz frequency range, in conjunction with the OI 630.0 nm optical flux calibrations.  We have used our data to explore possible explanations for CR Dra's persistent ECM emission, including its origins in magnetically-trapped particles and in quasi-stable flux caustics, in an attempt to explain its long-term persistence.  We have also derived a comprehensive timeline of CR Dra

Our cutting-edge visualization technique, articulated neural rendering (ANR),  allows users to generate photorealistic 3D avatars from just a few posed images of a subject's face or body. Unlike existing avatar creation methods that are often limited to specific domains or require extensive subject manipulation, our approach leverages a neural network to model subjects in any configuration and uses a minimal amount of images. When creating an avatar, users simply need a set of images of the subject in different poses, and our approach uses a single neural network to compute a sequence of subject configurations based on these images. Our technique can also automatically align images from different subjects, and our results show that it outperforms existing methods in both quantitative measures and visual quality, especially for challenging cases such as multi-person animations. To facilitate the development of applications that utilize ANR, we also release an open-source implementation based on the neural image processing framework (NIP) to complement this paper.

Humans and computers process images through identical visual senses but respond differently to image alterations. So far, research examining how much organisms and machines are affected by image transformations has been conducted separately, raising the question of whether these effects can be felt simultaneously by living organisms and computers.

In a study involving over 1.5 million ratings from over 38,000 humans, as well as over 18,000 ratings from a powerful computer model, we assessed how much various image distortions, such as rotations and translations, affect image quality perceptions.

Our analysis reveals a consensus between human and computer evaluations, with both showing a similar decline in sensitivity to certain image transformations. However, organisms and these advanced computer models exhibit differing levels of sensitivity to certain transformations that affect their performance equally.

The study offers a straightforward method for simulating the impact of image processing errors on living organisms, bringing us closer to understanding, for example, how much a cat's brain is affected by a blurred image.

Since this study delves into a fundamental aspect of image perception, the discovered results can be applied across the board to any point we wish to measure, offering a novel method to compare the performance of existing AI algorithms designed to emulate human vision and those that directly interact with computer images.

The representation of the U(2) algebra within a two-dimensional space and its relation to holonomies in both Euclidean and Lorentz spaces is examined. Specifically, this involves expressing the algebra as ad-operator combinations in the two-dimensional space, utilizing spherical monopole harmonics as wave functions. Following the representation's construction, the CS matrix is derived and, through the application of the Schrödinger equation, its eigenvalues are determined. Furthermore, the eigenfunction corresponding to the zero eigenvalue is identified. Additionally, the paper outlines a connection to the inhomogeneous rotation groups and spin representations of SO(3,1), and explores potential extensions to the Ponzano-Regge and Askey-Wilson recurrence relations relevant to relativistic quantum field theories.

Our study presents a comprehensive analysis of the ground state of the ( hydrogenated ) YNi$_2$(OH)$_2$C$N$ compound, investigated through a 2D quantum model derived from $\alpha$-Ln$_2$(OH)$_2$C$N$ (where Ln represents Sm or Er), combined with an experimental verification of its 2D quantum properties. We also examined the impact of hydrogen's replacement with another atom in the equivalent Ni-based compounds. Our computational model, accounting for disorder and uncertainty in the Ising-like spin interactions, showed that the quantum ground state of the system is characterized by spontaneous dipolar magnons in addition to the existing antiferromagnetic trigonal ordering. In contrast, the higher-coupling 90-degree twisted ferromagnets exhibit enhanced magnetic properties when the uncertainty is increased, reduced, or depleted. Yet, for the lower-coupling ferromagnets as well as the Er-based compounds, a less common phenomenon known as the low-temperature low-uncertainty spontaneous dipolar magnon occurs. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that hydrogen's replacement results in an increased low-uncertainty energy gap distinct from the existing high-uncertainty low-uncertainty energy gap. Pre-trained language models, exemplified by GPT-3, have exhibited an unexpected capability for zero-shot learning in various tasks without explicit training, albeit this ability is prone to dataset and prompt memorization and requires expertly crafted prompts. In order to make this capability more robust and accessible, we have developed a technique to create broadly applicable and easily transferable training data for few-shot learning. This involves automatically assembling multiple examples from a dataset into prototypical prompts that represent core features of the dataset. Subsequently, pre-trained language models can be fine-tuned on this training data, leading to superior performance in few-shot learning scenarios. In comparison to traditional tuning, our approach offers the advantage of making learning resilient to dataset memorization and significantly reduces reliance on prompts that were used during model training. Furthermore, since the assembled prompts lack specificity to individual datasets, this method renders the model resistant to prompt memorization. Extensive experiments have been conducted on 16 tasks, encompassing 6 domains, and demonstrate improved results in few-shot learning and zero-shot learning scenarios. Additionally, the technique is available in an open-source implementation.

In the context of the $Z_3$-invariant NMSSM, we examine the possibility of a first-order electroweak phase transition occurring, which would have significant implications for the $H_2$-dominant scenario. Beyond the constraints posed by the LHC and dark matter investigations, our results indicate that for the $Z_3$-invariant NMSSM, a first-order phase transition is only plausible when certain higgsino-like dark matter characters are relatively light. Furthermore, our study suggests that in the event of a significant phase transition occurring, the parameters are likely to be within a range that is testable using future gravitational wave detectors.

We introduce a novel approach for evaluating the frequency information of broadband millimeter-wave spectra to identify reliable redshifts for cosmic sources. Our approach, High-z Sudoku, utilizes detailed models of line and continuum emission to generate precise redshift estimates. The sensitivity of this method to various parameters, including noise levels, model complexity, and frequency ranges, is thoroughly investigated. Our study demonstrates that millimeter-wave (210-270 GHz) spectra with signal-to-noise ratios greater than 20 allow for the accurate determination of redshifts in excess of 6 with confidence levels exceeding 90%. Additionally, we apply our approach to two robustly detected millimeter-wave sources, AX J1644-14AB and 1E 0102-730, to derive redshifts of approximately 6.7 and 6.4 respectively. The associated spectral models are also presented in detail. Our approach is designed to be versatile and applicable to diverse millimeter and submillimeter spectroscopic datasets, making it a valuable tool for redshift measurements in this wavelength range.

To investigate certain quantum spin liquids, we employed the self-consistent continuous time quantum Monte Carlo method to study a $S=1/2$ Heisenberg antiferromagnet on the triangular lattice. We focused on the method's ability to sample all its spin configurations as a solution to the quantum Heisenberg model without making any approximations, exploring its numerical feasibility on smaller clusters. Our research involved calculating the energy per spin, spin correlation, and spin-spin interaction for various parameter settings within the $J_1-J_2-K$ model framework. We found that certain parameter regions exhibit increased energy per spin at absolute zero, indicating a symmetry-breaking state, as well as regions with lower energy per spin that do not indicate any symmetry-breaking state, potentially indicating a quantum spin liquid. We used our research to study a phase transition between two different symmetry-breaking states and compared our results to those from other theoretical approaches and experimental measurements on related materials.

Utilizing high-temperature lattice simulations of $SU(3)$ Higgs theory with two fundamental scalars, we investigated the relationship between Polyakov loop correlations and temperature. Our results show that at a specific temperature known as the deconfinement point, the range of correlations is inversely related to the number of loops. Furthermore, the strength of this inverse relationship increases as temperatures rise above deconfinement. We observed a contrasting behavior below deconfinement, where the range of correlations decreases as temperatures decrease. Based on these findings, we propose a model that effectively captures the transition from confinement to deconfinement, which could be extended to other gauge theories with multiple matter fields.

Cr2Al, a intermetallic compound with a tetragonal L10 structure, is of considerable interest on account of its high N\'{e}el temperature of approximately 263 K and unique properties as an antiferromagnet. Yet, particulars of its magnetic and electronic properties are yet unknown. Using neutron diffraction and reflection topography, the magnetic structure and arrangements of within the Cr sublattice at 10 and 250 K were identified. The data display an in-plane antiferromagnetic structure with coordination of in-plane magnetic sublattices at 250 K, aligning along the [001] direction. The parameters of magnetic structure at 10 and 250 K were calculated to be (0, 0, 0) and (1/2, 1/2, 0), respectively. The in-plane magnetic structure is composed of alternating ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic layers, with an in-plane magnetic structure showing wrap-around along the [001] direction. The exchange connections among neighboring ferromagnetic layers were found to be considerably feeble, whereas those among neighboring antiferromagnetic layers were found to be substantially robust. The exchange connections among neighboring ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic layers were found to be of comparable strength. A new kinetic model, the $\sigma$-model, is proposed which builds upon the model by Srinivasan et al., yet incorporates a variable collision frequency that adjusts based on velocity, thereby reflecting the intermolecular potential's effect. Specifically, the $\sigma$-model takes into account a hard-sphere potential, thus considering only elastic collisions. By assuming a Boltzmann distribution, the model's solution is derived for rarefied gas flows, both in planar and cylindrical geometries, using the linearized Boltzmann equation. By comparing theoretical solutions to exact Monte-Carlo simulations, the model's precision in accounting for potential effects, like attraction or repulsion, in rarefied flows is evaluated. Furthermore, the model's applicability is broadened by allowing collision frequency modulation, thus enabling accurate prediction of force laws with various exponents, even down to Newton's law for like particles. However, limitations arise when dealing with unlike particles, where attractive potentials or repulsive exponents greater than 4 lead to significant deviations from the Maxwell model, thus highlighting the need for model improvement in these scenarios.

Building upon the foundation of Natural Language Processing and semantics, a new area of study, Naturalized Semantics, seeks to create machine learning models that can accurately translate sentences into meaning representations the way a person with some basic education in linguistics and syntax can. However, natural language processing researchers have made little progress in this field. To bridge this gap, we've developed a new approach for translating sentences into meaning representations, using existing linguistics knowledge and a set of translation examples to create a common language for meaning and words. Our models, which are based on this common language, can then be trained using very little data, and accurately translate sentences despite having never seen the words in the context of a sentence before. We've demonstrated this breakthrough on a range of existing natural language semantics datasets, which were previously too small for machine learning models to work with effectively. Our models have shown significant improvements, which are confirmed through our experiments and by an in-depth examination of the models' ability to translate sentences.

Researchers are working on advanced silicon sensors for the Electron-Ion Collider, a powerful new tool capable of studying the fundamental components of matter. The collider will enable scientists to understand quarks, gluons, photons, and other subatomic particles with unprecedented precision, ultimately revealing the nature of matter and its components. By pushing particle interactions to the extreme, researchers can gain a deeper understanding of QCD and the forces governing subatomic particles. Advances in measurement techniques and precise calculations will allow the EIC to test key theories of matter and its interactions, including the Standard Model and potential beyond. The EIC will investigate key questions such as the partonic nature of nuclear matter, the strange quark, and other fundamental topics, using powerful beams of electrons, protons, and ions to promote new understanding of the underlying matter. The EIC's capabilities will encompass various interactions, including deep inelastic scattering, photon-glueball interactions, and other processes, ultimately promoting a new era of scientific discovery. The EIC's design will utilize a new, innovative concept based on a circular tunnel, where electron beams will interact with targets made of low-energy ions at specific points, using advanced magnetic fields to steer and focus particle interactions. The EIC's construction will utilize existing infrastructure at Brookhaven National Laboratory, with the potential to collaborate with other laboratories and institutions worldwide, ultimately promoting a new era of scientific discovery at an unprecedented scale.

A study of a low-mass AGN, located in the constellation of Andromeda at approximately 0.5 lackparsec from its nucleus, shows significant variability in X-ray and optical spectra over a period of about 160 years. The research indicates that the observed fluctuations could be the result of fluctuations in the accretion rate, suggesting an extremely low mass for the black hole, or they may represent the periodic expulsion of plasma, which would result in a significant decrease in luminosity following each eruption. The analysis of spectral data using X-ray and optical observations reveals a high level of activity, while the isolated X-ray flares observed during these years appear to be separate events. The duration of these X-ray flares ranges from two to six years, accompanied by notable optical brightness increases in two out of the three instances. The research observes that the X-ray spectra display a high level of hardness, with a significant fraction falling within the soft band, accompanied by a harder companion source, indicating the presence of multiple energy production mechanisms. The study of these X-ray flares leads to three possible models, including jet activity, absorption events, or emission due to high-energy particles. The observed low luminosity, coupled with rapid flux variations, indicates that the X-rays originate from a relatively small region. The comparison of variability on small and large scales in the X-rays shows that the X-rays originate from much closer to the black hole. Our research revisits the concept of convective dynamo and its implications for the magnetic field distribution across a star's radius using HD58260, an early B star, as a reference point. By utilizing high-resolution spectropolarimetry, we measured the magnetic field within specific spectral lines and discovered a substantial, positively inclined field, amounting to approximately 400 Gauss, as well as a significant, 0.7 radian per decade, radial decrease in field intensity. This observation aligns with theoretical models from simulations of magnetic field evolution, although the magnitude may vary based on parameters such as the micro-rotational coupling mechanism and whether the primarily influencing factor is turbulent or stable magnetic fields.

Utilizing the formula for vector fields acting on tensor products of one-dimensional free bosons, we derive a representation of the Dunkl operator's intertwining operator within the space of anti-symmetric functions of several variables. This representation's form demonstrates that the Dunkl operator's action on anti-symmetric functions can be equivalent to the action of a set of second-order differential operators on bosons, effectively reducing to the standard free boson differential equation for the special case of monomial functions. This equivalence reveals an interesting vector field representation of the Hecke algebra associated with the symmetric group, which is obtainable via limiting this representation to the symmetric group's action on symmetric functions. The derived bosonic representation of the Dunkl operator is also found to be applicable when working within the space of even anti-symmetric functions, leading to the identification of a second set of differential operators. Furthermore, this system is found to be equivalent to a free boson representation of the Hankel operator, which is obtainable via limiting this representation to the symmetric group's action on functions with a Hankel transform. The derived unitary Hankel transform is found to be equivalent to the standard unitary Hankel transform of the free boson system, which is obtainable via limiting this representation to the symmetric group's action on functions of this type.
