A new, systematic method, known as the Clebsch canonization, has been developed to simplify Lie-Poisson structures on the general linear group by translating them into Hamiltonian vector field equations on symplectic vector spaces, which can then be transformed into the geodesic flow of a smooth Riemann surface. This method has provided a group-invariant interpretation of the KdV and AKNS hierarchies. Furthermore, the method has been extended to Lie-Poisson structures of arbitrary rank.

Our study details the analysis of microlensing planets identified through one-dimensional light curve inversion methods from data collected in 2018 by the KMTNet network at microlensing fields that are considered sub-secondary to account for inner planets. Out of 60 detected planets from non-sub-secondary fields that were previously studied, 37 planets are confirmed through validated data and other constraints, whereas 23 require further validation. This research is the sixth reporting on a specific dataset and is designed to provide a comprehensive dataset of planets that are subject to external validation, covering six specific microlensing fields that are considered sub-secondary to account for inner planets. The final dataset of this report consists of 18 planets that are confirmed through validated data and represent half of all sub-secondary field planets from years 2018 that were analyzed. The report also provides an in-depth examination of several potential sources of bias that affect planetary findings, including those of secondary effects that are opposite to primary effects. The confirmation of a planet with mass similar to that of Neptune and an orbit of roughly 2 AU is particularly notable as it falls within a significant "neutron star - planet boundary" region, where theories based on yields from the formation of these stars indicate there should be very few, if any, planets.

This is the second installment of a series on developing novel methods to control the preservation of mathematical invariants, which is crucial for the accurate modeling of physical systems. By leveraging the finiteness of these conserved quantities within a limited timeframe, we establish a framework for the precise representation of flows that fall outside of the realm of classical mathematics. This is achieved through a novel extension of distribution theory. Building upon the methodological foundations established in the first paper, which focused on an ideal fluid model, we apply our approach to the more complex compressible Navier-Stokes equations, which govern the dynamics of fluids across a broader range of thermodynamic states. Ultimately, our approach provides a general solution to the challenge of accurately modeling physical systems, even when they exhibit solutions with highly oscillatory or multifractal properties.

Accurately predicting non-performing loans (NPLs) is vital for banks, as it enables them to assess client creditworthiness and adjust their strategies accordingly. Banks can make more informed decisions by leveraging machine learning algorithms that utilize diverse data, including clients' financial reports and behavior. Our study employs a real-world dataset from a commercial bank in Serbia to evaluate the performance of several machine learning models. Our objective is to identify the most effective model for NPL prediction and understand which data features hold the most significance. Upon conducting our analysis, we found that random forest models consistently outperformed other methods across five different evaluation scenarios. Additionally, our results indicate that bank employees' appraisals of clients play a crucial role in determining NPLs, as they often take into account factors such as the client's reliability and transparency.

The connections between the chromatic symmetric functions of Dyck paths, q-rook theory, and Pólya's Theorem are explored through the application of a symmetric function analogue of Newton's identities, resulting in two combinatorial interpretations of Lascoux-Schütbrian's chromatic symmetric function formula for walk structures.

Traditional invariance methods in computer vision were developed to withstand input changes along specific axes, yet real-world images respond differently to variations along those same axes in unpredictable ways. To address this issue, we delve into how deep networks naturally react to input direction changes and design our innovative model, Direction Convolution Networks (DirNet), which utilizes orthogonal direction convolution to capture direction-specific features. Additionally, we developed the Synthetic Direction Cosine Dataset to visualize a network's progression from being insensitive to input variations to recognizing different directions, and our results confirm DirNet's ability to do so. When tested on various image classification tasks, DirNet demonstrated equivalent or superior performance to state-of-the-art models, including improved accuracy on CIFAR ten-data sets and a notable 2.0% higher Top-1 accuracy on ImageNet 2012 when compared to VGG-16.

Using a novel relative trace formula, we investigate the theory of moduli spaces of linear connections, specifically on a Riemann surface of genus at least two, which exhibit an algebraic and symplectic structure that is linearized. This formula encompasses connections of various traceless orders, yielding an order parameter that significantly reduces the complexity of the associated arithmetic calculations. This enables us to compute an asymptotic expansion of the counts of these connections, up to a linear transformation, as the genus or order approaches infinity. Our findings demonstrate a profound alignment with periods from flat connections, which holds in multiple directions: locally (curved periods), within compactifications (essentially absolute), and within the broader relative setting. This relative trace formula marks a new advancement in the field, opening up further questions, such as tracing the relationship between periods of flat connections and their limits under certain compactifications within the moduli space of flat connections.

We investigate the impact of light quark masses on QCD gauge boson washout mechanisms that affect the electroweak phase transition (EWPT) and the lightest Higgs boson mass. Our study focuses on the role of QCD gauge boson mass terms in the $\bar{\theta}$-term and the electric dipole moment (EDM) of the neutron, as well as on the $SU(2)_L$ $\tilde{W}$ mass term in the EWPT. We found that under standard parameterizations of light quark masses, these effects become significant at the fourth order in these parameters. This analysis underpins a proposal for new precision calculations of these phenomena within chiral perturbation theory, specifically for the $\tilde{W}$ mass and the $\bar{\theta}$-term, to reduce dependence on unknown light quark masses.

Consider graphs $G$ that have an edge-coloring with $\ell$ colors, with specific restrictions on their structure. These graphs must incorporate a subset of vertices $M$, defined as the set of vertices in $G$ with relatively short odd multiplicative connections to the given coloring. These vertices must see an odd number of different colors, $\ell \neq 0$, within a relatively small radius, $2d + 1$. The study assumes that these graphs $G$ have nearly regular structure with a small degree difference, $|d_A - d_B| \le 1$. The research then focuses on a sequence of introduced subgraphs, $ (G_t, A), $ where $ A $ is a subset of vertices in $ M $ and $ t $ represents the number of new edges in $ G_t $ not present in $ G $ or in the subgraph $ A $. It then demonstrates a connection between the minimum number of odd cycles present in $ G $ and the value of $ t $, showing that $ \alpha(G) \leq \frac{\sqrt{2t+1}}{3} + 1 $. When the graph $ G $ has a subset of vertices $ M $ with specific odd multiplicative connections and a relatively small size, it shows that the minimum number of colors needed in an edge-coloring of $ G $ with these properties is $ O(\sqrt t)$ for the subgraph $ (G, M)

We have obtained a hypercontractive inequality for functions within the weighted Berman space built around the Bergman polynomial on the open unit disk, and similarly for its multi-variable extension on the polydisk. This inequality holds consistent symmetry and reveals the space's hyperbolic nature's impact on contractive factors. Moreover, we have confirmed an analogous inequality for the Bergman space on any domain with a non-negative analytic mean-type metric, and this includes the case of the polydisk. However, our attempt to prove a sharp hypercontractive inequality for the tensor product of multi-variable Berman spaces yielded only a sub-exponential increase in contractive factors compared to the expected result, and this limitation appears to be inherent.

Currently, most COVID-19 diagnosis methods either take too long (more than 4 hours) or require expensive and scarce RT-PCR tests. Imaging tests like high-dose X-ray scans can also lead to prolonged shortages of these resources. Consequently, developing a reliable physical model to detect the virus using low-dose computed tomography (LD-CT) is essential for both accurate diagnosis and preventing shortages of diagnostic and imaging resources. However, creating such a model poses significant challenges due to the limited spatial resolution of LD-CT scans. We present an innovative two-stage full-capacity capsule network that substantially increases the chances of being infected by focusing on distinct image details. Our method outperforms other methods by effectively identifying virus-carrying regions, thus reducing false and misleading readings. Notably, our model achieves a high overall infection rate of 93.4% while also maintaining an accurate false positive rate of 6.8%, surpassing other techniques.

In the past decade, numerous innovative satellite applications have been developed, leading to an increase in utilization of Low-Earth Orbit (LEO), but their actual usage still needs to be established. In order to grasp the current state of LEO space utilization, a thorough dataset containing 5475 space objects from 2000 to 2020 is examined in this study. An object investigation module is created and put to the test using this dataset, offering a systematic method for examining space objects based on their purpose. By analyzing various scenarios based on hypothetical needs of these objects, it's revealed that approximately 17% of them are actively employed in LEO, leaving around 83% without a designated function. In most scenarios, significant uncertainties surrounding the number of available free spaces exist, ranging from 6 to 18%. Furthermore, it's estimated that approximately 30 years will pass before every available LEO space is assigned a purpose based on the current rate of deployment. In most scenarios, significant uncertainties surrounding the number of available free spaces exist, ranging from 6 to 18%. In order to to clarify these findings, two possible explanations are presented, but these results hold steady under both interpretations. By analyzing debris mitigation efforts, it's expected that deploying new satellites at an extremely high rate could pose a challenge. In terms of space technology progress, it's expected that deploying new satellites at a moderately high rate could have an impact but it's expected that every available LEO space will assigned a purpose

To refine computer-aidly designed models for simulation, we create smooth meshes using quadrilateral shapes. Our method involves dividing the model into multiple regions and assigning points to create a smooth and consistent mesh. We use geometric constraints and optimize mesh characteristics like length, angle, and curvature using integer linear programming. Our method ensures a high-quality mesh with optimal length, particularly suitable for designing quadrilateral meshes. Experimental results show significant improvements over existing methods in terms of quality, feasibility, and compliance with original design features.

To develop more accurate statistical models, this research project focuses on calculating the distribution patterns, or statistical models, for various statistical measures, such as the sample correlation coefficient, using a large dataset. Initially, the study establishes a method to estimate confidence intervals for the sample correlation coefficient. Building on this foundation, it develops a computational strategy to generate the probability distributions, or statistical models, for multiple correlation measures applied to subsets of a given dataset. Subsequently, the study obtains general formulas for any desired level of subsetting accuracy. Ultimately, the study examines the efficacy of these statistical models using simulations.

We detail the Scattering Matrix Method, its underlying principles, and relevant formulas useful for calculating general metrics' properties, and examples are provided of how this method can be applied to models such as Einstein's, New Einstein, Whitehead's, and Telegravities, as well as to certain theories beyond general relativity involving deformations, modified actions, and higher-dimensional theories.

We investigate the stabilization of the 3D Navier-Stokes equations with no-slip boundary conditions in various spaces located within the critical L^q Sobolev and Besov spaces from February 2010 to April 2021. Utilizing novel control techniques, we demonstrate uniform stabilization in the B^s_{p,q}-L^q space under specific conditions, including 3 < p < ∞, 0 < s < 3 - \frac{1}{p} and q > 3. We also provide approaches for selecting the feedback controller and establish T^k_{X} L^q-orthogonality which contributes to this problem. Moreover, we explore the solvability of a finite dimensional optimization problem to demonstrate that a locally acting feedback controller is available in L^q spaces with 1 < q < ∞.

The LitMind Lexicon is a serviceable data set that can be used for tasks such as word representation, which was developed to provide references for single word meanings and to support the development of advanced language models that capture less common word meanings. The dictionary contains 21,973 entry words, each accompanied by five definitions and a synonym list, and these definitions have been used to create target sets for a number of words and to create context sets for their synonyms. The data set is openly available on GitHub at https://github.com/litmind/litmind-lexicon.

When diverse groups of people congregate online and are provided with product recommendations in real-time, the underlying decision-making processes often go undetained. Explaining these choices in an intuitive format poses a significant challenge, which can lead to reliance on simplistic algorithms utilizing local data. An innovative technique called LIME has been proposed to fill this explanatory gap by generating individualized explanations for recommended items. Although solutions like LIME break down complex decision-making processes into comprehensible components, they sometimes fail to account for users' individual perspectives, resulting in explanations that are generic and inaccurate. In response, we have modified LIME by incorporating user-specific features only, utilising residual reciprocal scoring (RRS) as the decision-making process. Through extensive testing across various online platforms and content types, our analysis reveals that LIME-RRS consistently provides relevant, coherent explanations that align with users' expectations. Furthermore, our research highlights that users of certain online systems prefer explanations revealing items similar to what was actually recommended, as well as those that were not, revealing an interesting dichotomy in preference between complete and partial explanation. These findings offer significant insights for designers of recommendation systems as to how and why explanations should be presented.

The electron spin resonance technique has been used to investigate the surface and near-surface layers of indium arsenide quantum wells. By varying the quantum well thickness and growing them on different crystal orientations, a unique interpretation of the electron spin resonance spectrum was possible, which is otherwise obscured by strong confinement effects in conventional studies. Our findings indicate that the surface of these materials exhibits exceptionally weak electron interactions, whereas the electron spins show an abnormally high degree of mutual interaction. This paradoxical coexistence of isolated and interacting electron spins presents an intriguing phenomenon that is challenging to explain through existing theoretical frameworks and offers valuable insights for the theoretical and experimental exploration of spintronic properties.

We examine how local inquiries into data reliability, implemented through classification boundary inquiries, can enhance training resilient models. By using an iterative prediction-correction approach, which incorporates these inquires, we can empirically show its effectiveness for classification under severe dataset corruption. In contrast, our findings also reveal scenarios where this method falls short of expected performance. A thorough analysis of the theoretical underpinnings will follow the presentation of experimental results.

Our previous research significantly sped up Sinkhorn iteration by taking advantage of a kernel matrix's inherent properties, transforming its computational complexity from $O(N^3)$ with naive Cholesky decomposition to $O(N^2)$ in a column-oriented data structure. This study further builds upon that concept by leveraging and improving two key aspects: full triangularization of a kernel matrix and an exact propagation of scaling factors. By doing so, we have developed an even more efficient algorithm known as Fast Sinkhorn II, achieving an astonishing $O(N)$ complexity in a block-wise data structure. This breakthrough renders the OT computation linear in terms of the number of data points, paving the way for applications in large-scale datasets. Moreover, we have created a highly efficient and generic C++ code for this algorithm, dubbed FastOT, which is designed to be portable, extensible, and user-friendly and incorporates the new $O(N)$ complexity algorithm. This study is backed by extensive numerical tests, which verify that FastOT surpasses various benchmarks, including benchmarks from prior literature and competing OT libraries, by a staggering factor. For instance, FastOT outperforms Sinkhorn3.0 by $50$ times when dealing with $N = 1,028$ data points across $13$ dimensions. Furthermore, our library has outperformed OTLib in numerous and significant tests where the former processed OT problems in $0.07$ seconds for $N = 19,756$ and $g = 44

Young stars like AU Mic are accompanied by planets and experiencing intense stellar activity, offering a unique chance to study active young Jupiter-like planets. A recent study using the AstroSat satellite of AU Mic's dormancy, flaring, and wind properties provided key data to determine the properties of its Jupiter-like planet, AU Mic b. Research confirmed that during dormancy, AU Mic's hot outer atmosphere is smaller than previously thought, and its stellar energy is largely absorbed by the upper atmospheric layers. Moreover, observations during a flare support previous findings that the planet's orbit lies within the flare emission zone. Additionally, stellar mass loss rates in the dormancy were significantly lower than in active states, and wind properties were more similar to those of other young stars, and the planet's orbital effects on its Jupiter-like counterpart were analyzed.

When an accelerated charged particle interacts with its surrounding medium, it experiences a counterforce due to radiation pressure, which is determined by the medium's conductivity and the acceleration of the charged particle. Our study examines this interaction between an accelerated charged particle and an impeded medium. Specifically, we investigate how this interaction impacts the particle's trajectory and discover that, beneath a certain threshold of drag force, the particle follows a quasi-ellipse path. As the drag force surpasses this limit, the particle's trajectory shifts to a cusp-shaped path. We also explore the electromagnetic radiation emitted by the charged particle as it navigates this cusp-shaped path and demonstrates that, despite intense local emission, the overall emitted energy remains minimal. Furthermore, we find that subtle alterations to the particle's initial conditions can, in theory, result in either negligible or massive loss of energy through radiation. To this end, we introduce a physical instance that illustrates this point: a star undergoing slow, spiraling rotation. In this scenario, we demonstrate that before the star's collapse, a minuscule adjustment to its initial conditions could potentially release an enormous amount of energy via radiation, which is substantially greater than its initial kinetic energy. Conversely, following the collapse, a comparable adjustment to the charged particle's conditions could result in an extremely diminished rate of energy loss despite the intense local emission.

The Classical Edgeworth Filter, an asymmetric version of the Classical Edgeworth Algorithm, is evaluated for its efficacy in high-dimensional imbalanced supervised classification tasks. This method initializes the nearest neighbor with positive class labels and iteratively assigns Class-0 labels to selected negative neighbors based on an optimized filter function. We demonstrate that the Classical Edgeworth Filter is a versatile optimization technique that can be applied to diverse neighbor selection algorithms, notably including the Optimal Filter, a renowned algorithm developed by Dasgupta. We then propose the Classical Edgeworth Filter-based K-nearest classification algorithm, which combines the optimized filter function with a neighbor selection strategy. Furthermore, we explore a Dynamic Majority Vote variant of this algorithm, capable of enhancing performance in somewhat balanced datasets. We validate the effectiveness of these innovative approaches through rigorous threshold tuning and high-dimensional imbalance assessments on the dataset inter arrivals from the Google Paired City dataset.

Our analysis combining SkyMapper drift scan survey and Gaia DR3 data has expanded the collection of bright, distant quasars, almost doubling the quantity to seventeen between z=5.5 and z=6.5, with particular emphasis on an ultra-bright quasar, HbS J2346-0441, at a redshift of z=6.282, with a remarkable apparent brightness of 19.11 magnification-corrected magnitude in the SDSS i-band. Our updated understanding of the distribution of bright, distant quasars now indicates that the number of quasars per unit redshift per unit flux, the luminosity function, has a different relationship with luminosity at a steeper rate than what was previously predicted by any quasar population model in this region of the Hubble universe. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the average intervening redshift of the quasars used in our analysis is around z=2. Both the DR3 Gaia and the SkyMapper databases have contributed to a significant enhancement in our understanding of the relationship between the number of quasars per unit flux and redshift, particularly in how this relationship changes with luminosity, with new ultra-bright quasars found at a redshift range of z>5.5. These newly-discovered quasars have helped to shift the understanding of the relationship between the number of quasars per unit flux and redshift, particularly in how this relationship changes with lumin

We have successfully observed the initial charging of an isolated superconducting island attached to a single quantum dot, going from a hybrid metal-insulator state, by utilizing radio-frequency sensing with gates. Our analysis reveals that in addition to standard charging and discharging behavior, there are two significant mechanisms for charge tunneling: normal and superconducting processes that are distinct due to the quantum dot's ability to sense charges. We found that the quantum dot's sensitivity to the island's state allows us to determine when a single excess electron transforms into a superconducting Cooper pair under the influence of a driven degenerate mixing (DDM) phenomenon. Moreover, our work enables us to accurately identify the points at which the two tunnel couplings between the quantum dot and the reservoirs become equal, resulting in a shifting transition between charging and discharging behaviors that is driven by applied gate voltages.
This research focuses on the interpretation, expansion, and refinement of the concept of contraction towards entropic discontinuities within the context of conserved system equations.

We explore novel view synthesis, particularly extended and long-term view generation, which challenges traditional methods due to changing conditions like illumination and weather. To address this, we present a robust approach based on diffused image prior, enabling the synthesis of new views beyond what's initially captured without any external constraints. To enhance reliability, we incorporate a conditioning scheme that utilizes multiple scenes captured at different times. By combining this with a time-consistent reconstruction constraint, our approach significantly improves the robustness of view synthesis. Notably, our method performs well even in the presence of significant scene changes and extended time gaps, outperforming other state-of-the-art long-term view generation techniques and conditional diffusion models.

Many complex systems are composed of numerous interconnected components. Analytical methods for these systems often prove difficult or impossible to develop, yet data from various perspectives can be leveraged for predictive modeling and optimization. This paper proposes a novel approach based on a long-short term memory (LSTM) neural network framework that combines multilayer perceptrons with an attention mechanism, enabled by the employment of multi-view data. This method is demonstrated through its application to the networked infectious disease model, achieving effective prediction and optimization using only local system information. Furthermore, it is also used for control purposes after some adjustments. Additionally, comparisons with relevant models and an analysis of viewing angles are presented.

The instability and breakup of a liquid layer on a fiber when subjected to a distant irrotational flow, such as during airblast sprays in nuclear accidents, can be explained using a simplified theoretical model. This model reveals that as the liquid layer thins, the instability grows more rapidly and the resulting droplets are smaller in size. Specifically, the characteristic droplet diameter is inversely related to the slip coefficient and directly related to the velocity of the external flow. Our theoretical predictions match recent experimental findings on water droplets formed by high-pressure air sprays.

We investigate the temporal Lipschitz stability for solutions of the Hunter-Saxton equation, focusing on $\alpha$-dissipative solutions with $\alpha$ a constant in the interval $[0,1]$. We introduce and study the properties of metrics both in the Lagrangian and Eulerian frameworks. By constructing specific distance-preserving maps between Lagrangian Lagrangian coordinates and Eulerian phase space, we achieve metric Lipschitz stability for solutions in the Eulerian framework. Moreover, when the solutions possess smoothness, we define and calculate metrics both in the Lagrangian Hamiltonian and energy variables, and then establish corresponding Eulerian metric Lipschitz stability results, also taking into account the transport term. These metrics, in addition to providing stability results, can also be utilized to quantify the distance between solutions with potentially different Lagrangian manifolds.

A new, fully automatic ultrasound assessment method, using robotic scanning with ultrasound, has been developed to measure the curvature of the spine from external images. This technique requires minimal patient cooperation and can be used in conjunction with a conventional ultrasound machine. To test its reliability, our study compared the spinal curvature measurements obtained from robotic scanning with those from traditional manual scanning. Spinal curvatures were also measured using X-rays, serving as a reference point for validation. A total of 60 individuals with scoliosis participated in the trial, and multiple external images were taken from each participant using both robotic and manual scanning techniques. Computational algorithms were used to analyze these images and calculate spinal curvature metrics, such as S$_{ultrasound}$ and S$_{XR}$, which were then compared across multiple groups of participants and measurement repetitions. Our study demonstrated strong reliability metrics, including high coefficients of agreement (range: 0.774 to 0.879) and little variation among repeated measurements (average coefficients of variation: 0.073 to 0.135). Furthermore, robotic scanning was found to produce reliable results that were in line with those measured by manual scanning and supported by X-ray data. These results suggest that robotic scanning may be a viable option for assessing spinal curvature in individuals with scoliosis, as it provides reliable data that is on par with both manual scanning and X-ray images.

This paper introduces an efficient technique for modelling spoken word durations in linguistic frameworks that don't incorporate duration information. A significant challenge in creating synthetic durational patterns is establishing a meaningful unit of measurement that accurately captures average or typical word durations. To overcome this, we developed a median-based approach that uses non-parametric statistical methods to model durational patterns by treating each word as an independent event with random durations. A compact binary code representing durational patterns is then created and used to generate synthetic instances. Experimental results show that our method significantly reduces the size of durational data compared to traditional approaches, making it more feasible to create high-quality synthetic data sets. Moreover, our method is just as effective as more complex approaches in generating realistic durational patterns in speech synthesis.

This research investigates the application of hate speech identification techniques that are both quick and in-depth, utilizing an extensive dataset harvested from the micro-blogging platform Twitter in an effort to grasp the context of online abuse. We gather more than 60,000 tweets, categorizing them as either offensive or not, and then broke down the data into training, testing, and validation sets. We explored the effectiveness of 13 distinct feature selection techniques in enhancing the performance of seven different machine learning models. The outcomes indicate that feature selection significantly improves the accuracy of these classifiers, with the highest success rates observed for methods that utilize information theory, such as Relief F and MRFCM. Additionally, our results show that ROC-AUC is the best performance metric for our binary classification task. It's worth noting that our experiment's outcomes may be influenced by the limitations of our dataset.

Multi-Object Detection with Multiple Input and Multiple Output (MIMO) has emerged as a highly promising technique for handling complex data. Although significant advancements have been made to enhance its performance, a major issue persists where Individual Neural Network (NN) networks tend to specialize in either capturing local features or maintaining global feature fidelity. As a result, their collaborative efforts are often hindered by inconsistent feature representations. To overcome this limitation, our method focuses on leveraging the representational similarity of feature maps within each NN to enhance their shared feature extraction capabilities. Consequently, this leads to improved overall accuracy. Notably, when incorporated into the popular Faster R-CNN (Region-Based Convolutional Neural Network) framework, our approach yields exceptional results across standard benchmarking datasets, notably in the Microsoft COCO challenge.

Text extraction from historical manuscripts is a complex task full of challenges due to varying handwriting styles, fragile condition, and passage type. Diverse collection formats, spanning thousands of years, add to the difficulty of extracting useful information. Scholars from multiple domains such as history, literature, and archaeology rely on extracting information from these manuscripts. Despite the state-of-the-art text analysis techniques available, applying them requires overcoming language barriers, and achieving accuracy in accurately translating the content poses significant logistical hurdles. Given the state of current machine learning technology, identifying objects within manuscript images poses a significant problem for semantic applications. Due to the scarcity of high-quality, annotated datasets, researchers have to compromise on test sets or create their own. Historically significant, handwritten manuscripts often only have limited transcription available to them. Due to the limitations of current transcription technology, only a small fraction of manuscripts have been digitally represented. Considering the state of current machine learning technology, training effective models for text feature extraction poses significant problems due to the scarcity of suitable datasets. This study provides an extensive review of available historical manuscript image datasets, discussing their characteristics and potential applications. Although there are numerous datasets, they primarily serve as base models for training and evaluation purposes. Due to the limitations of current semantic recognition technology, only a few "baseline" datasets are available for training. Due to the constraints of time and resource availability, only a small selection of datasets meet a certain standard of quality. This study addresses these limitations by including a discussion of datasets requiring resource allocation

This study presents a straightforward mechanism to enhance the precision of flatness-based robot joint control utilizing secondary encoders. The proposed approach relies on measuring the differences between readings from the primary and secondary encoders, transforming this information into an error signal, and then adjusting the joint movement speed to minimize this error signal. The development of this method is motivated by the existence of significant slippage in some encoder readings during movement, specifically in robotic joints equipped with harmonic drives. Experimental findings involving a robotic arm movement from its natural position to zero on all axes showed that the proposed controller achieved zero total cumulative error over the course of eight cycles. Moreover, comparisons between this novel controller and a similar adaptive flatness-based control system developed by M. Magni et al. in 2019 revealed that the proposed controller resulted in zero cumulative error over repeated movements and significantly reduced offset errors compared to the adaptive control method.

This study examines the course of health over time in individuals who suffered a first myocardial infarction, based on a comprehensive dataset containing 14 years of health records. This extensive dataset includes data on hospitalizations, physician visits, medication, and medical treatment for related conditions such as ischemic heart disease, atrial fibrillation, dyspnea, and peripheral artery disease. A key aspect of this analysis is its consideration of cumulative risks and multiplicative models of joint risks, all aimed at improving the understanding of how simultaneous health issues impact an individual's overall health trajectory. Furthermore, this approach incorporates dynamic life course regression models, examining the dynamic effects of multiple time-varying factors, such as depression, physical activity, and risk factor control, on subsequent events. Ultimately, this method enables the development of effective prevention strategies focused on managing co-occurring health issues and their underlying causes.

A novel computational method, known as Multi-Center, has been developed to analyze the behavior of atoms and molecules when they interact with a fluid environment. This approach, which models the electron cloud as a collection of discrete regions, is unlike traditional continuous methods used in density functional theory. By projecting individual site points onto localized atomic orbitals using pseudo functions, the Multi-Center method enables efficient handling of long-range electrostatic interactions. This approach is particularly appealing due to its simplicity and low computational cost compared to other methods. As such, it has been successfully applied to a wide range of molecules and ionic liquids, yielding results in line with established methods including density functional theory and quantum chemistry. Furthermore, it has been demonstrated that it can also be used to calculate the diffusion of molecules and ions in water with minimal adjustments to the underlying code.

A subset of vertices forms the metric dimension of a graph, allowing any two distinct vertices to be uniquely identified with minimum distance between them. Specifically, we investigate the time complexity of finding a maximum subset of this metric dimension, parameterized by the size of another subset of vertices (denoted as $P$) and by the number of certain structured components within the graph (P, H, induced H-ind induced, and feedback vertex number). Our analysis reveals that determining a maximum subset of this metric dimension, parameterized by the size of $P$ and the number of induced H-ind components, is an NP-hard problem. However, we establish a parameterized time complexity of $2^{O(k^2)} \cdot n^2$ for the well-defined case of P = H = induced H-ind = induced H, primarily due to the restriction that the metric dimension itself must be contained within $P$. Additionally, we show that determining a maximum subset of this metric dimension, parameterized by the number of induced H-ind components and the size of $P$ (equal to the number of induced H-ind components or to 3), is an W[1]-hard problem when the primary parameter under consideration is the size of $P$ (equal to the number of induced H-ind components or to 3). Directed spaces, which have a distinct notion of direction compared to topology, allow for the generalization of topological spaces in various topological categories. This notion of direction gives directed spaces unique properties that make them distinct from topological spaces. The equivalence between directed spaces and \chi-spaces, and the directionality of topological spaces, raise the question of generalizing topological spaces in directed spaces. This paper explores this idea by defining special types of directed spaces, called H-spaces and χ-spaces, and demonstrating their relationship with filtered spaces. The properties of these spaces are further investigated, and the article establishes the correspondence between them and the properties of topological spaces. The article also defines several concepts, including directed maps, equivalence of directions, power frameworks, and the interaction between them. This leads to the definition of directed maps in χ-spaces, and the article proves that these maps form a category. The article also discusses the relationship between the properties of directed spaces and the properties of their directions.

To understand future climate scenarios, we investigate extremely warm and humid climates as we increase CO2 levels. Our research focuses on the Amazonas region, where high CO2 levels could lead to the water cycle becoming unstable, resulting in heavy precipitation and potentially harsh living conditions for humans. We used a computer model to study these climates and found that they can support life due to a atmospheric process that prevents the climate from becoming too cold. However, our study also found that these climates still experience a significant decrease in solar energy, resulting in moderate temperatures. We discovered that high CO2 levels result in deep clouds, which block solar energy but encourage precipitation. The model suggests that these climates are generally stable, but sudden changes in the climate can occur, resulting in more intense precipitation and flooding. Our research found that these climates have a limited range, extending from -30 to 60 degrees latitude, and that they are found on the western sides of planets.

We have developed an approach to higher-spin Yang-Mills theories and its self-dual counterpart in twistor space, following the method that Corichi and Yee adapted from Merkulov, which involves integrating a characteristic class. This strategy is versatile and applicable to other gauge theories. By taking the self-dual sector as an example, we demonstrate that the twistor space calculations for free Yang-Mills theories become straightforward. Moreover, our method allows us to explore the relationship between Yang-Mills theory and its self-dual sector in twistor space. Additionally, we have explored the extension of this approach to (A)dS2 Yang-Mills theory, which has significant implications for quantum gravity research. This analysis could potentially lead to valuable insights into the properties of gravity theories.

The application of deep neural networks in medical image classification has been widely recognized due to their advanced image mapping capabilities. Despite this, current deep learning-based methods have limitations when dealing with noisy real-world medical image labels, where a single flawed label within multiple, conflicting options can significantly impair the model. To address this issue, we propose an innovative method that utilizes Bayesian statistics to improve and maintain the accuracy of image labels, ensuring the model's robustness and long-term reliability. Experimental results on medical datasets demonstrate that our method effectively mitigates the impact of noisy labels, even in complicated, high-noisy scenarios. Furthermore, when applied to out-of-distribution situations, the model's performance is enhanced, and variability is reduced.

This article provides fresh estimates for the norm of a projection operator
established in interpolating splines with a quadratic smoothness property.

A connected graph G links associates a corresponding random walk, which is defined by a transition probability matrix P. It is established that a p-matrix can be constructed from the eigenvalues of a depleted P, corresponding to states with zero probability. This p-matrix characterizes the transition probability matrix P. 
The unitary equivalence between depleted transition probability matrices and a prolonged transition probability matrix demonstrates that a characteristic polynomial derived from P is equal to the determinant of a matrix formed by concatenated rows and columns of P. 
As an alternative, this result provides an integral expression for the n-th coefficient of the characteristic polynomial of P. 
Additionally, this equivalence leads to a condition under which a graph's eigenvalues and eigenstates can be determined from its Fiedler vector and eigenvalue. 
An example illustrates a situation in which a unidirectional cycle in a hypercube is characterized by a characteristic polynomial derived from P, yet the corresponding prolonged P exhibits distinct eigenvalues, each with a non-zero Fiedler vector.

In this work, we propose a theory of time-based functionality, and we develop a formal framework in HOL to model this concept. This framework provides a basic structure for defining the behavior of systems over time. We introduce a non-terminal language construct for recursive function definitions that can be reinterpreted to accommodate time-based changes in functionality. We establish a fundamental theorem, proving that initializations, functional relationships, and exclusivity form a valid basis for functional structures. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach within a theoretical context, we define two time-based interpretations of the factorial function.

This study presents a novel, data-driven method for enhancing the predictive capabilities of coherent structure-based models of wall-bounded turbulent flows. Such models can generate high-resolution flow data by post-processing numerical simulations or using data analysis techniques, which can then be used to "heal" or "augment" instantaneous predictions made by the original models. This is done by ensuring that predicted wall shear stress or velocity values align with those in the high-resolution flow data. We demonstrate and evaluate this new approach using data from both homogeneous, isotropic turbulence and the log-layer of wall-bounded turbulence at specific distances from the wall. Our findings indicate a significant general improvement in the accuracy of the prediction models, particularly for large-scale structures, which is consistent with the characteristics of the high-resolution flow data. What's more, the method shows exceptional potential for optimizing the performance of models by allowing for the adjustment of several parameters that control how much predicted flow data is "incorporated" into the augmented predictions.

We've modified the Skyrme model, incorporating a born-invariant term with a
infinitesimal lambda coefficient. By taking the limit where lambda approaches
zero, we maintain the target space dimensionality but impose the condition that
the Skyrme coupling remains non-zero and stays constant. The energy functional,
when reduced to its lowest dimensions, reveals a three-dimensionality with terms
based on both curvature and magnetic fields. Within this framework, we identify
self-dual solutions, thereby establishing a set of non-rigid, rotating, topologically
non-trivial solitons. We also establish a relationship between the magnetic field
and curvature through an inverse square law, specifically at a magnitude of
(4/3) * Pi * Pion mass * Curvature radius. These solitons are stable in nature.

By combining a specific type of Berry curvature dipole and twist, we identify a new quantum state that emerges in a two-dimensional twist gapped Weyl semimetal when subjected to a periodic and strength varying magnetic field. At certain values of the field, areas with high and low magnetic strength alternate in a pattern that creates localized areas of high charge density. We discovered that as the size of these regions increases with the number of twists, their charge density becomes independent of the magnetic field's configuration. Using the capacity of these regions' twisted and spin-locked electron states, we propose a way to control electron flow and store information in a magnetic device that doesn't block electron movement, opening the possibility of creating a new storage technology. Due to its stability against magnetic disorder, this approach could lead to the development of reliable and scalable storage technologies based on twisted and gapped metals.

This research paper proposes a unique optical nanoantenna consisting of a hybrid dielectric-plasmonic structure that integrates a resonant silicon nano-disks array coupled to a thin GaAs nanomembran e. The innovative design leverages the advantages of both silicon and GaAs materials to achieve an advanced optical system. By combining the technique of nano-fabrication for silicon nano-disks and wafer-scale fabrication for GaAs nanomembran e, the new nanoantenna can be realized with a high yield and high uniformity. Our investigation demonstrates that this new nanoantenna can efficiently enhance the emission of single photons and entangled photons from GaAs nanomembran e, as well as support the propagation of entangled photon pairs beams in a controlled and directed manner. Ultimately, the new dielectric-plasmonic structure holds great promise for the development of efficient, luminous and unidirectional photon sources in the near-infrared range.

We've studied the Coulomb interaction in granular matter, which shows an unexpected screening behavior due to the inherent dielectric loss and conductive properties of granular assemblies. Contrary to commonly assumed pure dielectric loss, our research shows that logarithmic Coulomb decay is a better fit for the observed interaction between charged particles in these conductive media, which is supported by both experimental and computational findings. Additionally, we used theoretical calculations based on anomalous screening theory to understand how the decay rate is influenced by variables such as temperature, grain size, and distance between charged particles, and these predictions were confirmed by experiments and computational models simulating screened Coulomb interactions in granular matter.

Using density functional theory, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of Mn-silicene units in relation to their structural, energetic, and magnetic properties. We evaluated various configurations of Mn on 4H-BN substrates with different helical twist angles. Our research demonstrated that Mn on 4H-BN is more stable in a bilayer structure with a relatively small twist angle of 10.26 degrees. We discovered that Mn-silicene units exhibit semiconductor characteristics depending on the twist angle. The unit exhibits a direct bandgap at smaller twist angles and a indirect bandgap at larger angles. Our research showed that Mn-doped silicene units on 4H-BN can potentially be tuned to exhibit quantum anomalous Hall, Dirac, and topological insulator states. We investigated this using tight-binding models, where we found that Mn-doped silicene units on 4H-BN have the potential to be used in various spintronics applications and could also be engineered to achieve phase transitions between different band topologies.

The Sgr A East radio source is a 10,000-year-old molecular cloud that was formed after a massive star explosion near the center of the Milky Way, particularly around a massive OB association called the \omega Centauri system. To determine the creation time of Sgr A East, we need to find when the cloud became ionized. By analyzing spectral data from the ATCA telescope, we calculated the Sgr A East's velocity relative to LSR, finding a high-velocity wing on the west side and a blue-shifted wing on the east side, implying that the supernova occurred about 10,000 to 20,000 years ago, with Sgr A East expanding at 1000 km/s. However, our research shows that the supernova occurred between 7 to 15 million years ago, with expansion occurring at 64 km/s, and the ionization happening between 10,000 to 20,000 years ago, with expansion occurring at 1000 km/s. Sgr A East could have been formed by either a 60 M$_\odot$ red supergiant or a 30 M$_\odot$ Wolf-Rayet star, depending on which OB association member the supernova originated from. Our research suggests that the supernova occurred either from the massive OB stars in \omega Centauri or from a compact OB association surrounded by the expansive cloud. Overcoming class imbalance in text classification can be achieved through methods that oversample the minority class or undersample the majority class. Our research focuses on oversampling techniques, which enhance the minority class to match the size of the majority class. These methods use synthesized text instances rather than actual ones to avoid introducing noise into the data. Our study evaluates and contrasts three state-of-the-art oversampling techniques to determine which is most effective for improving the performance of a text classifier. Conducted using multi-class datasets, the results show significant enhancements in the overall model's performance.

This study examines how local online news in the U.S. responded to the COVID crisis in terms of coverage, impact, and audience behavior. We first analyze changes in local news coverage of COVID across the U.S., exploring its connection to the virus's severity, government actions, and population characteristics. Using a sample of nearly 900 U.S. cities, we find a significant positive correlation between COVID-related local news coverage and COVID case and death rates. However, we also discover that government actions to combat COVID reduce local news coverage, lower their case and death rates. Next, we investigate the role of local news in informing audiences about COVID, focusing on pre-existing habits of local news consumption and demographic characteristics. We find that local news consumption is linked to greater awareness of COVID rules and lower case and death rates. Finally, we assess how audiences' responses to COVID are influenced by changes in local news coverage. Using a difference-in-differences analysis across cities, we find that an increase in local COVID news coverage leads to a decrease in COVID case and death rates, indicating that audiences respond to local news by altering their behavior.

High-precision simulations, particularly those in astrophysics, fluid dynamics, and magnetohydrodynamics, heavily rely on accurately conserving angular momentum due to its crucial significance. In cases where both magnetic and rotational forces are present, maintaining a stable, accurate, and precise angular momentum can be challenging, necessitating specialized computational methods. This difficulty is compounded when utilizing the conventional fast multipole method, which fails to preserve angular momentum, often leading to significant errors, even in the most controlled scenarios. In response, we have developed a set of optimized methods that not only ensure the exact calculation of angular momentum but also achieve this with minimal computational overhead. In various tests, we have found that our approach accelerates convergence towards exact results, while outperforming the standard FMM in terms of computational efficiency.

Despite the $e \vec {p} \to e \vec {p}$ reaction being one of the most thoroughly examined processes in the field of particle and nuclear physics, research continues to yield insights on the underlying physics. The statistical fluctuations associated with the electromagnetic properties of the proton play a crucial role in the cross-quadrant transition of polarization between the initial and final protons. Specifically, the statistical fluctuations affiliated with the target proton's electromagnetic field induce a transfer of polarization, which is in proportion to $\alpha^4$. Furthermore, our calculations reveal this phenomenon to be distinct from the previously studied phenomenon of (quasi-)diffraction.

In a scenario where a learner lacks initial knowledge about its environment, it must rely on expert guidance to make decisions. However, if those experts' rules are unknown, the best strategy for the learner is to imitate the experts' past actions, which requires identifying the underlying patterns in those experts' actions. Typically, this task is manageable when experts receive comprehensive training, involving an extensive number of samples. Unfortunately, most existing theories and algorithms are designed specifically for such situations. To address this limitation, this research investigates a more realistic environment in which experts' training data are relatively limited, after which they provide their services to the learner. To tackle this problem, the study suggests employing a conditional generative adversarial network (CGAN) to generate additional, albeit fake, actions from the experts in the initial phase. By doing so, the learner can learn more effectively with the augmented data. Building on a new identification procedure for experts' distribution, which relies solely on expert actions, the study enables the determination of experts' training data distribution and, subsequently, the generation of fake actions in the experts' training epoch. Interestingly, the study demonstrates that under this new setting, the learner can achieve nearly accurate action prediction. Consequently, the learner can acquire the experts' policies at a relatively high rate, which approaches optimality when the experts' training data are sufficiently extensive. To characterize this transition, the study introduces two distinct communication thresholds, which separate the two regimes. To validate the theoretical analysis, the study proves

A study by the ATLAS collaboration at the Large Hadron Collider, utilizing a dataset with an integrated luminosity of 139 inverse femtobarns, investigated the production of Higgs boson pairs alongside a vector boson. These processes, predicted by the Standard Model, incorporate a range of production mechanisms including vector bosons of charged nature. To pinpoint the desired signals, analysts relied on the tracks of charged particles, multiple jets, and two or more gamma-ray pairs, among other signatures. Signals derived from non-standard physics with pairs of Higgs bosons accompanied by vector bosons were also examined for their relevance to the observed data. Specifically, these signals were analyzed by matching expected numbers of events to the observed results in the range of backgrounds, ultimately resulting in limits imposed on the relative probabilities of their occurrence, with limits imposed being up to 262, 409, and 610 a trillion, for W, Z, and $\gamma$/Z Higgs boson pair production respectively, with the exception of the $\gamma$ vector boson signal which had more lenient requirements with the limits imposed being up to 425 a trillion, with the requirement of the precise mass of the Higgs boson pairs set at 124 GeV.

Our study showcases the development of an extremely stable laser system, powered by less than 20 specific atoms, and features a precision time cycle that can be adjusted with ease. This innovation is built upon a digital laser concept that was initially proposed in 1992. The realization of such a miniature laser system presented a significant technological challenge, requiring the simultaneous improvement of three key components: highly stable atomic clock operation, accurate atom manipulation, and precise detection of their collective behavior. The achievement of this milestone brings us closer to the realization of a digital laser as initially envisioned.

For K3 surfaces with an automorphism having a Siegel disk, we prove that the associated period matrix occupies a Siegel disk if and only if it represents 0 in the moduli space. Furthermore, we demonstrate that if a K3 surface contains a Siegel disk, its period matrix cannot lie within a Siegel disk; this outcome is achieved by showing that the period matrix's Siegel disk homology is distinct from its Siegel disk cocycle space. These findings are complemented by two examples.

In the context of the dark matter's annihilation process within the galactic center halo, a specific scenario involving the neutralino's decay into real chargino and neutralino pairs is explored. Since neutralinos are no longer considered the lightest supersymmetric particles by recent LHC findings, this decaying state becomes a feasible option. With a mass range of 400 to 600 GeV for the neutralino, as well as varying mass splits between charginos and neutralinos, this study examines the resultant gamma ray production. A notable finding suggests that in instances where the mass difference is less than the neutralino's mass, the primary decay product is two-body decay, resulting in gamma ray spectra characterized by distinct features. Conversely, when the mass disparity is greater than the neutralino's mass, the neutralino decays into three-body products, resulting in characteristic end-point patterns. A potential detection method for such decaying states could involve identifying signatures of monochromatic or doublet gamma ray emissions at rates greater than background standards, particularly within the galactic center or sun, although the latter may be subject to cosmological constraints. A comprehensive list of predicted gamma ray rates is provided for various mass conditions, and could serve as a recognition marker for such decaying states if detected in the gamma ray spectrum.

We develop a randomized algorithm that efficiently approximates the genus of a given graph, yielding a positive outcome with a high degree of certainty. Specifically, for any graph with n vertices and genus g, the algorithm yields an approximation in the range of $O(g\cdot(\log\log n)^2)$ with an extremely low failure probability of $2^{-\Omega(g)}$. A key transformation enables the same method to accurately approximate the surface genus of a dense graph with $n$ vertices and genus $g$, yielding an approximation in the range of $O((\sqrt{2\pi g}+\sqrt{g})\cdot\log n)$. Additionally, we introduce a new concept called "black-box" which simplifies our approach and is expected to be a useful technique in the future, yielding an approximation scheme that is fully independent of the graph's explicit representation.

A persistent challenge in network communications is ensuring balance between the quantity of data transmitted and the number of data packets, particularly when carrying out distributed optimization tasks. While reducing the quantity of data, we must ensure convergence to the optimal solution. This paper presents a novel algorithmic solution to the problem of distributed convex optimization, using a stochastic gradient approach to minimize communication while maintaining convergence to the optimal solution. Furthermore, we address the issue of data accuracy and develop a simple, linearly convergent solution. Additionally, we investigate the performance of our approach by examining the characteristics of communication requirements and solution accuracy. These concepts are further illustrated in a distributed sensor network application.

This research investigates the application of advanced neural networks to classify hate-speech in two popular Indian languages, Hindi and Bengali. Given the languages' similarities with English, yet having distinct grammatical and syntactical characteristics, we delve into an in-depth analysis of the prediction accuracy. Additionally, we find the best model to train and how to transfer it to low-resource languages for effective hate-speech identification. To achieve this, we collected and labeled an extensive dataset of over 109,000 social media posts from Hindi, Bengali, and Gujarati, offering an in-depth analysis of the subject matter. It is crucial to note that the dataset does not promote hate speech but rather serves as a resource to understand hate speech patterns on social media, aiming to promote love and unity among people from diverse backgrounds on social media. An accurate model is derived by experimenting with various neural network configurations, incorporating word and character levels, and utilizing manual and learning-based methods for handling undefined words. Furthermore, we explore the effectiveness of transfer learning in two distinct ways, namely by training the model with a similar language, and by training the model with a vast dataset of English text. Interestingly, our research reveals that the model's performance degrades when dealing with undefined words, and highlights the influence of dataset size and word encoding methods on hate speech patterns in the studied languages. Ultimately, the proposed model is tested on an unlabeled dataset and evaluated using metrics such as AUC and F1, providing an insightful analysis of hate speech

In high-precision detectors like the LUXZeplin dual-phase experiment, minimizing nuclear recoil recoils in the dark matter particle candidate is a significant concern. Although recoil detection is inherently challenging due to the event's subtlety and the detector's inherent noises, advanced timing information can significantly aid in this endeavor. With the aid of a timing-based analysis, this study investigates how differences in event types - either signal or background - can be discerned through both charged ion timelines and total ion timelines, also making use of full timelines for improved accuracy. Various definitions of observables, including those based on time and combining timing and energy information, are proposed and evaluated in terms of their capability to differentiate between signal and background events. Notably, this study finds multiple definitions that can reliably separate signal and background incidents below keV energy thresholds. Moreover, simulated data from multiple prototype experiments demonstrate that these definitions can significantly reduce background occurrences below the keV threshold, minimizing false positives. Overall, this study provides crucial information for operating Time Projection Chambers at low energy sensitivity, particularly in the field of dark matter particle detection.

The widespread adoption of autonomous driving is seen as a precursor to a broader transformation of commercial vehicle operations, where trucks and vans are integrated into the larger e-commerce network. As part of this process, various non-navigational tasks such as package delivery planning and vehicle routing are being automated using machine learning models. However, recent research indicates that these automated solutions can sometimes produce unfair outcomes, sparking the need for new, more refined methods of validation and improvement.

Our study focuses on the challenge of enhancing the efficiency of automated commercial vehicle routes in urban environments. Through a large-scale experiment involving 100 e-commerce experts, we analyzed the impact of moderating the decisions made by machine learning models with the help of context-specific knowledge. The results revealed that integrating human expertise at an individual level, particularly through written feedback, was able to significantly boost the efficiency of automated routes in complex and highly customized scenarios. 

This research is the first to explore the role of written feedback in improving the navigation capabilities of commercial vehicles. Our results suggest that by combining machine learning and human intelligence, we can create more responsive and efficient automated systems, tailored to the specific needs and requirements of commercial transportation.

A new type of competition, the Out-of-Category challenge, was held alongside ACMM 2022, where participants received fresh CASIA IR images for eye disease diagnosis, but with a twist. To raise the bar, participants were restricted from using their usual training datasets, forcing them to adapt to a unknown dataset. Our team participated in this challenge by first examining the iris quality in each category. An iris image classification system was then developed to optimize accuracy and minimize errors. Building upon this foundation, we successfully overcame the limitation of limited training data and inaccurate disease labels by implementing corrective measures in our model's training process. As a result, our system's accuracy in healthy iris detection surpassed that of the competition average, and error rates were significantly reduced.

Random fields are commonly used as models for multivariate functions in different fields of study. Mathematical tools for analyzing these fields are often developed as theoreies, but often, specific applications require computational methods. This study focuses on the geometric representation of random fields, treating them as the surfaces of complex, probability-distributed shapes called Gaussian manifolds. This statistical structure is utilized to identify geodesic paths within these complex shapes. Initially, the study defines a resampling technique that approximates the shortest paths between any two points on these complex shapes. Then, the study demonstrates the efficiency and accuracy of this method by applying it to two practical cases from different fields. Firstly, the study shows its potential in learning processes through a simulation of a robot that learns to navigate through unfamiliar spaces. Secondly, the study reveals its potential in genetics through a simulation of the evolution of complex traits in organisms.

This note examines reconnection in birefringent fluids through the observation points, lengths, and lengths squared, using numerical simulations in a 2D slab model. It's discovered that the reconnection speed is capped at a lower level than the local sound speed due to these observations points. Defined reconnection rates based on the lengths or lengths squared show periodic behavior similar to the energy in fluids with a non-unity birefringence parameter. However, the sign of the periods and amplitudes differ compared to various phases, and the direction of growth or decay changes at specific times. Ultimately, the reconnection rates defined by lengths or lengths squared converge to a consistent expression independent of the birefringence parameter, allowing for a unified description of reconnection across different fluid models.

For a modular form $f$ of even weight $2g$ and its associated Dirichlet series $L_f(s)$, defined using the Fourier expansion of $f$, we examine specific values $L_f(1-s)$ where $s$ represents the imaginary part of the first $2g$ zeros of the modular form $E_{2g}$ associated with the even elliptic modular form. We establish a lower bound on the absolute difference between $L_f(1-s)$ and its nearest integer, proving that this difference is bounded as $f$ varies within a given neatness class as long as $s$ remains fixed. This finding generalizes previous work by Matevus and we provide supporting examples. We also address unique scenarios where $s$ approaches zero and show that $L_f(1-s)$ does not necessarily yield an integer at a rational number near but not equal to 2. This outcome is particularly significant in the particular case where $s$ equals the imaginary part of the weight 12 Dirichlet series associated with the modular form $\Delta$, yielding an infinite series of numerical values for $L_f(1-s)$. This particular case resolves in part the conjecture of Shokurov regarding an elliptic curve. A supporting result for further study is provided where we study $L_f(1-s)$ for all $f$ within a given neatness class as $s$ approaches zero. This work is realized within the framework of the

In a study on the transport of electrons and spin currents in armchair graphene nanoribbons, using the non-equilibrium Green's functions method within the tight-binding framework, we investigated how these processes are influenced by the width of the nanoribbon. Our research found that the transport of electrons and spin-like currents through these graphene nanoribbons exhibit distinct patterns determined by their transverse momentum states. These results imply that the flow of spin-like currents can be manipulated by controlling the width of the nanoribbon, thereby offering opportunities to develop devices that regulate spin currents based on momentum principles.

This paper presents proofs in a Korovkin style for a class of multi-dimensional linear and weakly nonlinear, monotonic operators acting on vectors of functions that are smoothly bounded and have compact support within a multi-dimensional space. We derive convergence theorems for certain types of linear and nonlinear operators that preserve or do not preserve probabilities and are applied to various statistical physics models, including a diffusion model with impenetrable disks, a multi-dimensional hard-sphere model, a soft-sphere model, and a model for particle interactions on a plane from the theory of interacting particle systems.

A set of vertices in a graph is defined as pancyclic if it contains a cycle of any length from 3 to n, where n represents the total number of vertices in the graph. Researchers study a problem introduced by Galvin in 1983, aiming to determine if it's possible to achieve a partition of the graph's vertices where each subset's size is relatively close to the previous, and this subset's neighborhood is completely connected to the previous one, with both being independent sets. Initially, the problem's solvability was explored for specific types of graphs with a bounded diameter. It was proven that a certain type of graph with a diameter of 2 can only have two independent vertices or one vertex attached to both, when applying a specific partition. It was also concluded that a more complex graph structure, with a diameter of 2 and a maximum degree of 4, can only have 4 vertices in total or 3 vertices where one is connected to both, when achieving a partition of independent vertices. Furthermore, it was confirmed that a set of 8 vertices does not satisfy the condition of having a partition of the graph's independent vertices, while allowing a cycle of 3 in the neighborhood. However, it was also confirmed that a set of 7 vertices does satisfy the condition of having a partition of the graph's independent vertices, with a cycle of 3 in the neighborhood.

Our study calculates the directed flow of various hadron species in gold, gold with neutron excess, and other nuclei collisions at a high energy density. We used the EPOS3 model to simulate these interactions and found that it effectively accounts for the formation of quark gluon plasma in a wide range of hadron types, based on their distinct properties and the way they interact with the medium. We then analyzed and compared the behavior of different hadron flows in various collisions and observed significant differences that could provide further evidence for the presence of quark gluon plasma in extreme natural occurrences.

The adaptive spectral Koopman method was designed to solve complex autonomous dynamical systems that serve as the groundwork for numerous applications in physics and engineering. It utilizes a data-environmental approach to identify low-dimensional coherent structures within chaotic systems in their native state, facilitating the reduction and approximation of highly complex differential equations into more manageable partial differential equations or ordinary differential equations in lower dimensional spaces. Two major variants of the ASK method have been developed: the first using Smolyak's technique for efficient numerical integration, and the second leveraging tensor product sparse grids to optimize this method. We introduce a new approach, sparse-grid-driven ASK, which capitalizes on sparse grids for an even more efficient and versatile method. We apply SASK to the simplified two-dimensional vortices system, the hyperbolic system on the annulus, the rotating convective instability, and the quasilinear system mimicking a wind-tunnel experiment, demonstrating its superior performance in terms of computational efficiency compared to traditional collocation-based ASK methods. We analyze the effects of various parameters such as tensor structure, refinement, and ad-hoc parameters on these methods using an in-depth numerical study. The results indicate that SASK outperforms traditional ASK methods by adapting to the underlying structure of the problem without additional computational cost. It provides a more efficient and robust approach that can handle problems with different tensor structures and gradients without the need to adapt or adjust any parameters, making it a promising tool for solving a wide variety of complex

The Outer Complex Scaling Technique has been successful in finding wave functions for atomic and molecular systems that interact strongly with a uniform electric field. The O CST method's ability to converge smoothly towards strong field limits has been demonstrated in a number of cases. The O CST method converges well because it can treat strongly interacting electrons by scaling potentials outside the outermost region of the wave function properly, thus preventing unbounded solutions. This understanding led to new Outer Complex Scaling Variants being developed. The O CST method's convergence properties will be examined for a range of atoms and molecules interacting with uniform electric fields. The Outer Complex Scaling Approach's generalisation through a technique called 'projected' methods will also be explored. The Lippmann-Swinger framework was used to create a theoretical understanding of resonance widths using the Outer Complex Scaling Approach. The Outer Complex Scaling Approach was successful in creating equations that describe time-dependent wave functions that show exponential decay beyond a certain point, thus accurately modelling the physical phenomenon of resonance widths.

The Sinkhorn algorithm is widely used for computing the optimal transport between two probability distributions. Although it converges in most cases, there are exceptional circumstances in which it does not. Specifically, we have found that when the optimal transport does not exist due to insufficient coupling between the distributions, the algorithm may enter an infinite loop. Moreover, we have discovered that even when the optimal transport is unfeasible because of insufficient coupling, the algorithm still converges toward a cycle that depends on the scaling factor used in the projectors. By analyzing these unusual behaviors, we have gained a new understanding of the algorithm from a theoretical perspective.

The combined measurement of the top quark pair cross-section in $pp$ collisions at $\sqrt{s}=5.02$ TeV from ATLAS and CMS is reported. Using data from 2017 with integrated luminosity of 257 pb$^{-1}$, a combined measurement of the $t\bar{t}$ cross-section, accounting for electronic and di-leptonic decays, yields $\sigma_{t\bar{t}}=43.7$ pb, with a 0.8 pb uncertainty. This combined assessment exhibits an satisfactory agreement with the theoretical calculations based on next-to-leading order QCD and electroweak predictions.

We study a coupled system consisting of an ultracold atoms and an optical cavity.  This system can be described by the Hubbard model under coupling to bosons.  Our analysis reveals that it exhibits two distinct non-equilibrium many-body states: light-induced insulator and light-induced metal.  These states demonstrate unique light and matter correlation properties as well as distinct self-similar patterns.  Furthermore, the system exhibits a critical point at which it displays self-bound droplets of glassy state, featuring self-similar patterns and non-local behavior.  These findings demonstrate the potential for an optical cavity to induce novel phases of matter in Hubbard systems, even in simple configurations.

This research aims to incorporate generalised Bessel functions into the Janowski class, a subset of starlike functions, by applying Hankel determinants and linking them to extreme theory. It also investigates relationships between the coefficients of conformal mappings.

Urban settings are known for fostering diversity and opportunities for city inhabitants to interact with individuals from diverse backgrounds; however, the COVID-19 pandemic significantly disrupted these dynamics.
